stem: A client gives a manager full discretion over a retirement account and cannot watch the trades in real time. Which statement best captures why ethical conduct matters in that relationship?
choices: The client must trust the manager with assets and private information the manager could misuse.
Ethical conduct matters only after a statute assigns a cash penalty to that exact trade.
A written compliance manual removes any need for the manager to exercise judgment.
explanation: Investment clients hand over assets and information they cannot fully monitor. Trust is what makes that handoff possible. A manual and the law both matter, but neither watches the order ticket at the moment it is placed. The strongest choice is: The client must trust the manager with assets and private information the manager could misuse.

stem: Colleagues debate whether investment management is a profession or only a skilled job. Which feature best supports calling it a profession?
choices: A shared duty to put client interests first, together with standards the community can enforce.
Pay that is higher than the median household income in the manager’s city.
The daily use of market-data terminals and valuation spreadsheets.
explanation: Specialized skill is necessary for the work and is not the feature that creates a profession. A profession adds a public-facing duty, shared standards, and a way to discipline members who break them. Software and pay do not create that duty. The strongest choice is: A shared duty to put client interests first, together with standards the community can enforce.

stem: A portfolio manager asks whether a practice is acceptable because no statute forbids it. Which comparison of law and ethics is most accurate?
choices: Ethical standards bind a professional only after a legislature copies them word for word.
The law is a floor. Ethical standards can require more than a statute spells out.
If a statute is silent, the conduct is automatically ethical.
explanation: Legal rules are the minimum governments will enforce. A practice can clear that floor and still abuse a client’s trust. Professions write standards for the gap between “not illegal” and “worthy of the assets clients leave behind.” The strongest choice is: The law is a floor. Ethical standards can require more than a statute spells out.

stem: Harbor Glass could legally vote client pension proxies the way a corporate client prefers. No statute requires a different vote. The merger Harbor Glass wants to support would hurt the pension beneficiaries who own the shares. Which reading is the best ethical conclusion?
choices: Ethics applies to trade recommendations only, so a proxy vote is outside the topic.
Legality ends the analysis, because law and ethics are the same test.
The vote can be legal and still be unethical if the beneficiaries’ interests are sacrificed.
explanation: This is a legal-but-unethical pattern. The statute does not forbid the vote, yet the people who bear the result are the beneficiaries. An ethical review still asks whose interests the manager was trusted to protect. The strongest choice is: The vote can be legal and still be unethical if the beneficiaries’ interests are sacrificed.

stem: A practical framework for ethical decisions in investment work starts before anyone picks an action. Which first step is the most useful?
choices: Identify the facts, the people who will be affected, and the duties owed to each of them.
Adopt the action the most senior person in the room already prefers.
Estimate only the effect on this quarter’s revenue and stop the review there.
explanation: A usable framework slows the decision down: what happened, who is affected, and which duties already exist. Starting from a boss’s preference or from near-term revenue skips the facts that make the choice ethical rather than merely convenient. The strongest choice is: Identify the facts, the people who will be affected, and the duties owed to each of them.

stem: Once the facts and the duties are on the table, which step best belongs in the middle of an ethical decision framework?
choices: Prefer the action that would be easiest to conceal if a client later complains.
Set out more than one possible action and compare how each action treats the affected people.
Announce a decision immediately so the meeting can end.
explanation: The middle of the framework is where alternatives do their work. The obvious path often serves the decision maker. Writing down other actions makes the tradeoffs visible before anyone is committed. The strongest choice is: Set out more than one possible action and compare how each action treats the affected people.

stem: A manager makes a decision, carries it out, and files the memo. Which later step still belongs in an ethical decision framework?
choices: Skip reflection because a completed decision cannot be undone.
Reflect only if a regulator opens a formal case.
Reflect on what happened and on what should change the next time a similar choice appears.
explanation: Reflection is how a framework improves the next judgment instead of repeating a miss. The point is not to pretend the past is editable. The point is to notice which pressures distorted the choice. The strongest choice is: Reflect on what happened and on what should change the next time a similar choice appears.

stem: Jonah Ellis’s bonus at Piper Street Capital depends on this month’s new advisory fees. A confused prospect is ready to sign for an unsuitable, high-fee product. Jonah tells himself he will “fix the allocation next quarter.” Which challenge to ethical conduct is most evident?
choices: Situational pressure from the bonus and the clock, which can crowd out the duty to the prospect.
The absence of any statute anywhere in the world that mentions investment products.
The lack of any decision framework anywhere in the investment profession.
explanation: The uncomfortable feature is not a missing statute. It is the bonus, the deadline, and the self-serving story that harm can be repaired later. Those situational influences are a common reason capable people slide into poor decisions. The strongest choice is: Situational pressure from the bonus and the clock, which can crowd out the duty to the prospect.

stem: A senior portfolio manager tells a junior analyst, “Send the rosy performance slide. I will take responsibility.” The junior knows the slide omits losing accounts. Which influence is most likely to push the junior to send it?
choices: Obedience to authority, treating a boss’s instruction as a substitute for one’s own judgment.
Too much reflection completed before the slide was drafted.
A careful comparison of duties owed to every client who will see the slide.
explanation: Obedience shows up when an order from someone with power replaces the analyst’s own review. A real framework would put the clients who will be misled back into the decision, even though the boss spoke last. The strongest choice is: Obedience to authority, treating a boss’s instruction as a substitute for one’s own judgment.

stem: Every trader on the Westmill Fund desk routes a slice of each client order to a high-cost broker and calls it “the relationship.” A new trader is told not to be the only person who refuses. Which influence does that comment rely on?
choices: Conformity, the pull to match the group’s practice rather than examine it.
An excess of independence from both clients and colleagues.
A legal rule that every broker must be paid the same commission.
explanation: The comment does not claim the routing helps clients. It claims that standing apart will feel uncomfortable. Conformity can make a weak practice look normal simply because the desk has repeated it. The strongest choice is: Conformity, the pull to match the group’s practice rather than examine it.

stem: An analyst says, “I am careful and experienced, so I would notice if I were about to do something unethical.” Which limitation of that belief matters most?
choices: Overconfidence about one’s own ethics hides situational pressure while it is happening.
Experience cancels conflicts of interest.
Careful people are exempt from duties to clients.
explanation: Experience helps and does not replace a look at the facts. A self-image of being a good person can become the whole analysis and skip the stakeholders and the awkward alternative. The strongest choice is: Overconfidence about one’s own ethics hides situational pressure while it is happening.

stem: A chief investment officer’s memo frames a decision only as “maximize this quarter’s asset growth.” Client constraints never appear. Which description of that framing is most accurate?
choices: A decision that mentions revenue cannot have ethical consequences.
Framing effects matter in consumer ads and not in professional judgment.
Narrow framing can hide the ethical content of a choice that is written up as a pure business calculation.
explanation: Once a choice is labeled as ordinary business optimization, duties can fade without anyone feeling they chose to do wrong. Putting the clients and the constraints back on the page returns the ethical content. The strongest choice is: Narrow framing can hide the ethical content of a choice that is written up as a pure business calculation.

stem: After clients lose trust in a well-known adviser, which consequence is the most direct threat to that adviser’s future business?
choices: Ethical failures increase trust, because clients prefer aggressive managers.
Clients withdraw assets and prospects stop referring friends because they no longer believe the firm will act for them.
Bid-ask spreads on every unrelated stock immediately fall to zero.
explanation: Trust is the asset an advisory firm actually sells. When it breaks, money clients were willing to leave in the firm’s care leaves too. That is a business result, not only a moral complaint. The strongest choice is: Clients withdraw assets and prospects stop referring friends because they no longer believe the firm will act for them.

stem: Capital markets move savings toward projects savers cannot run themselves. Which statement best links ethical behavior to that role?
choices: Savers commit capital only if they believe the people in the market are not systematically misleading them.
Allocation is faster when disclosure is optional and enforcement is rare.
Ethics and capital formation are unrelated subjects.
explanation: The social payoff of a market is that strangers fund one another. That funding shrinks when participants expect to be misled. Ethical conduct is part of how the market works, not a slogan beside it. The strongest choice is: Savers commit capital only if they believe the people in the market are not systematically misleading them.

stem: A compliance officer gives an analyst a checklist and says the boxes are enough. Which responsibility remains with the analyst?
choices: The analyst still owns the judgment when the checklist does not match the facts in front of her.
The checklist moves ethical responsibility to the person who printed the form.
Checklists have no proper place in an investment firm.
explanation: Compliance tools are help, not a stand-in for the professional. Unusual facts are where a checklist runs out and the duty to think remains with the person who sees those facts. The strongest choice is: The analyst still owns the judgment when the checklist does not match the facts in front of her.

stem: Two actions are legal. Action A pays the manager more this year and leaves the client in an unsuitable product. Action B pays the manager less and fits the client’s written needs. Which ethical conclusion is the strongest?
choices: Profit to the manager is the definition of an ethical outcome in a business.
Ethics always requires the least profitable action, even when the client is unharmed.
The more profitable action is not automatically the ethical action.
explanation: Ethics is not a claim that profit is suspect, and it is not a claim that profit settles the choice. In this pair, the distinguishing fact is harm to the client. A higher fee does not repair an unsuitable recommendation. The strongest choice is: The more profitable action is not automatically the ethical action.

stem: A firm prints a code of conduct and then pays teams only for asset growth, with no questions about how the assets were won. Which observation is most accurate?
choices: Incentives can defeat a printed code when the firm pays for conduct the code claims to forbid.
Compensation design sits outside professional ethics.
A printed code guarantees behavior no matter how people are paid.
explanation: People respond to what the firm actually rewards. A code contradicted by the bonus design teaches staff which document is real. Culture includes pay, not only the poster in the lobby. The strongest choice is: Incentives can defeat a printed code when the firm pays for conduct the code claims to forbid.

stem: A manager is deciding whether to accept a new client. Which stakeholder list is the most complete starting point for an ethical review?
choices: The prospect, existing clients, the employer, and the market’s interest in honest advice.
Only the manager and the manager’s family.
Only a regulator that might someday read the file.
explanation: A short stakeholder list produces a short decision. The prospect can be harmed, existing clients can be crowded or used to subsidize the new relationship, the employer carries reputation risk, and dishonest advice makes the market worse. The strongest choice is: The prospect, existing clients, the employer, and the market’s interest in honest advice.

stem: An analyst sees a colleague backdate a performance chart and thinks, “Someone else will report it.” Which challenge does that response illustrate?
choices: Excessive obedience to the client’s written investment policy.
A reasoned conclusion that backdating helps the beneficiaries.
Diffusion of responsibility, in which each bystander assumes another person will act.
explanation: The analyst has not decided the chart is acceptable. She has decided that action is someone else’s job. In a profession, that drift is how a known problem stays in the file. The strongest choice is: Diffusion of responsibility, in which each bystander assumes another person will act.

stem: A long client relationship has become a personal friendship. The client asks for a hidden exception to the firm’s allocation policy. Which tension should the ethical analysis name first?
choices: Friendship automatically outranks every professional duty.
Personal relationships are irrelevant because ethics covers only strangers.
Loyalty to a friend can collide with duties owed to other clients and to the employer.
explanation: Difficult cases are often mixed loyalties rather than cartoon villains. Naming the collision keeps the other clients in view instead of letting affection finish the analysis. The strongest choice is: Loyalty to a friend can collide with duties owed to other clients and to the employer.

stem: Which description of ethics is the most useful for an investment professional?
choices: A private mood about whether someone feels guilty afterward.
A catalog of investment products that a regulator has already approved.
Shared principles that guide conduct when a contract or a statute does not settle the question.
explanation: Feelings can be a signal, but ethics in a profession is a shared guide other people can discuss and apply. An approved-product list is regulation, not the whole of ethics. The strongest choice is: Shared principles that guide conduct when a contract or a statute does not settle the question.

stem: A new hire says, “If it is in the client contract, it is ethical, and if it is not in the contract, it is a personal matter.” Which correction is most appropriate?
choices: A contract can set duties, and professional ethics can still impose duties the contract never mentioned.
Contracts become unenforceable as soon as a code of ethics exists.
Professional ethics applies only to people who have no contract with the client.
explanation: A contract can omit a duty, stay silent, or try to waive a protection the profession still expects. Ethical analysis does not end on the signature page. The strongest choice is: A contract can set duties, and professional ethics can still impose duties the contract never mentioned.

stem: During a market panic, a supervisor says, “There is no time for the usual process. Do what I did in the last crisis.” The junior has not checked whether the client’s limits have changed. Which pairing of challenges is most accurate?
choices: Obedience to authority together with time pressure.
Too much reflection and an excess of stakeholder mapping.
Too much independence from the client’s instructions.
explanation: Two influences operate at once. The supervisor’s old habit is treated as an order, and the panic is treated as a reason not to read the current mandate. Both are ordinary situational pressures, and they stack. The strongest choice is: Obedience to authority together with time pressure.

stem: Why does a profession publish a code instead of relying only on each member’s upbringing?
choices: Upbringing is identical across a global membership, so a code is only ceremonial.
A code removes the need for judgment in individual cases.
Clients and colleagues need a common standard they can learn and expect from people they have never met.
explanation: Investment work crosses countries and firms. Strangers will not share one childhood. A code gives them a public benchmark and still has to be applied with judgment to facts the code did not narrate. The strongest choice is: Clients and colleagues need a common standard they can learn and expect from people they have never met.

stem: A manager discloses a conflict clearly, and the client still hires her. Which statement about trust is most accurate?
choices: Honest disclosure can support trust because the client judges the conflict instead of discovering it later.
Once a conflict is disclosed, it can have no further ethical significance.
Disclosure reduces trust, so conflicts should be hidden when the client is likely to agree.
explanation: Trust is not a claim that conflicts never exist. Trust is a claim that the professional will not hide them. Disclosure lets the client decide. Some conflicts should still be avoided rather than only described. The strongest choice is: Honest disclosure can support trust because the client judges the conflict instead of discovering it later.

stem: An employee is told that refusing a questionable instruction will cost her a promotion she has pursued for five years. Which feature of situational pressure is the most precise?
choices: The cost of doing the right thing is personal and immediate, while harm to clients is easier to minimize.
Promotions are unethical by nature.
Pressure exists only when the instruction is illegal on its face.
explanation: Situational pressure works by making the personal stake vivid and the client’s harm abstract. The promotion is not itself the ethical problem. The problem is letting that near-term personal cost erase the duty. The strongest choice is: The cost of doing the right thing is personal and immediate, while harm to clients is easier to minimize.

stem: Which statement about an ethical decision framework is most accurate?
choices: It is used only inside compliance departments, not by investment staff.
It is a repeatable way to slow down, compare duties and alternatives, act, and learn from the result.
It is a formula that produces one numerical score for every moral question.
explanation: The framework is a discipline, not a calculator and not a department. Investment staff meet the facts first. Its value is that the steps exist before the bonus conversation starts. The strongest choice is: It is a repeatable way to slow down, compare duties and alternatives, act, and learn from the result.

stem: A client says, “I hired you so I would not have to think about the trades.” Which professional implication is most accurate?
choices: The client’s delegation increases the manager’s responsibility, because the client is not watching each ticket.
Trust is unnecessary when the client is wealthy.
Delegation cancels the manager’s duties, because the client waived attention.
explanation: Discretion is the condition that makes trust, care, and loyalty the product. Wealth does not restore the client’s view of every order. The strongest choice is: The client’s delegation increases the manager’s responsibility, because the client is not watching each ticket.

stem: A team follows its ethical decision steps and still faces two lawful actions that affect stakeholders differently. Which description of the remaining task is most accurate?
choices: Disagreement inside the team proves the framework failed and should be dropped.
Judgment is still required. A framework structures the choice and does not erase it.
If two actions are lawful, they are ethically equal and the team should flip a coin.
explanation: A framework keeps relevant facts on the table. It does not force thoughtful people to weight those facts identically. The remaining work is judgment, and disagreement can mean the alternatives were actually considered. The strongest choice is: Judgment is still required. A framework structures the choice and does not erase it.

stem: Which example is the clearest case of conduct that is legal and still a failure of professional trust?
choices: Recommending a high-fee product that fits a sales contest better than the client’s stated needs, in a place that does not regulate that advice.
Following a stricter local rule that the home office finds inconvenient.
Refusing to sign a filing the employee knows to be fraudulent.
explanation: The sales-contest recommendation can sit inside the law and still abuse the client’s reliance. Refusing a fraudulent filing and following a stricter local rule are examples of upholding duties, not of a legal-but-unethical failure. The strongest choice is: Recommending a high-fee product that fits a sales contest better than the client’s stated needs, in a place that does not regulate that advice.

stem: Why should a professional expect ethical challenges even at a firm with a strong reputation?
choices: Pressure, obedience, and self-interest show up in ordinary weeks, not only in scandals.
Reputable firms hire people who are incapable of conflicts.
Challenges arise only in countries that have no securities regulator.
explanation: Ordinary incentives cause ordinary failures. Waiting for a scandal means noticing the problem after a client is harmed. A good reputation is an asset to protect, not evidence that judgment can be switched off. The strongest choice is: Pressure, obedience, and self-interest show up in ordinary weeks, not only in scandals.

stem: A candidate asks how the Code of Ethics relates to the Standards of Professional Conduct. Which description is most accurate?
choices: The Code states broad principles. The Standards turn those principles into more specific duties.
The Standards are optional illustrations, and only the Code can be the basis of a violation.
The Code binds exam graders only, and the Standards bind portfolio managers only.
explanation: Members and candidates are expected to live up to both. The Code is the short statement of professional ideals. The Standards are the organized duties used to judge conduct. Treating the Standards as optional would empty the practical rules. The strongest choice is: The Code states broad principles. The Standards turn those principles into more specific duties.

stem: How are the Standards of Professional Conduct grouped?
choices: One undivided duty of confidentiality and nothing else.
Three groups only: research, trading, and marketing.
Seven groups: professionalism, market integrity, duties to clients, duties to employers, analysis and actions, conflicts, and responsibilities as a member or candidate.
explanation: The Standards are organized into seven broad groups so a duty can be found by the relationship it protects. Confidentiality is one client duty inside that structure, not the whole of it. Research, trading, and marketing are activities that cut across several groups. The strongest choice is: Seven groups: professionalism, market integrity, duties to clients, duties to employers, analysis and actions, conflicts, and responsibilities as a member or candidate.

stem: Who is required to follow the Code and Standards through CFA Institute’s professional-conduct system?
choices: Every employee of every investment firm, whether or not they are members or candidates.
CFA Institute members and candidates in the CFA Program.
Only people who already hold the charter, not candidates.
explanation: The Code and Standards are the professional rules for members and for candidates in the program. Candidates are covered before they hold a charter. People who have never joined and are not candidates are outside that membership system, even if other law still applies to them. The strongest choice is: CFA Institute members and candidates in the CFA Program.

stem: Which statement best captures, in ordinary words, one of the broad ideas of the Code of Ethics?
choices: Put the integrity of the profession and the interests of clients above your own interests.
Put the employer’s sales target above both the client and the law.
Put personal compensation first whenever a client has signed a fee schedule.
explanation: One idea in the Code, restated without quoting it, is that the profession and the client come ahead of the member’s private gain. A signed fee does not reverse that order, and a sales target does not outrank the client or the law. The strongest choice is: Put the integrity of the profession and the interests of clients above your own interests.

stem: Which statement best captures another broad idea of the Code, again in ordinary words rather than a quotation?
choices: Use care and independent judgment when analyzing investments, recommending them, and acting for clients.
Adopt the opinion of the firm’s largest trading counterparty whenever time is short.
Treat independence as a private preference that clients are not entitled to rely on.
explanation: Another idea in the Code is careful, independent professional judgment in analysis, recommendations, and related work. Outsourcing that judgment to a counterparty’s preference, or treating independence as optional, cuts against that idea. The strongest choice is: Use care and independent judgment when analyzing investments, recommending them, and acting for clients.

stem: A mentor summarizes the Code for a study group and wants one accurate plain-language idea. Which summary fits?
choices: Act with integrity toward paying clients and treat everyone else as outside the Code.
Reserve respectful conduct for people who already hold the CFA charter.
Act with integrity and respect toward the public, clients, prospects, employers, and other people in the markets.
explanation: A core idea of the Code reaches past the current fee-paying client. It includes prospects, employers, colleagues, and other market participants. Charter status is not the test for who deserves honest dealing. The strongest choice is: Act with integrity and respect toward the public, clients, prospects, employers, and other people in the markets.

stem: Which plain-language statement best reflects the Code’s concern with markets and society, rather than only with a single client account?
choices: Support honest and viable capital markets because society depends on them to move savings to real users of capital.
Support any market practice that raises this quarter’s assets, because society benefits whenever assets rise.
Leave market integrity to regulators, because the Code addresses only private client files.
explanation: One idea in the Code looks past the single account to the market people share. Asset growth achieved by misleading that market is not what the idea protects. The duty is not delegated away entirely to regulators. The strongest choice is: Support honest and viable capital markets because society depends on them to move savings to real users of capital.

stem: Which plain-language statement best reflects the Code’s idea about competence?
choices: Competence is fixed on the day a person passes an exam and needs no further attention.
Only a supervisor has any responsibility for competence.
Keep your own professional competence current, and help other investment professionals keep theirs.
explanation: The Code’s competence idea is ongoing and shared. Passing an exam is not a permanent substitute for staying capable in the work one actually does, and the duty is not limited to people with a supervisory title. The strongest choice is: Keep your own professional competence current, and help other investment professionals keep theirs.

stem: A charterholder says the Code requires only that she personally avoid fraud. Which missing idea is the most important correction?
choices: The Code also expects professionals to encourage others to practice in a way that reflects credit on the profession.
The Code forbids speaking with colleagues about any ethical question.
The Code applies only during the week of the exam.
explanation: Personal avoidance of fraud is not the whole Code. Another idea is to practice ethically and to encourage others to do so, so the profession’s reputation is more than one careful person. Silence toward a colleague’s misconduct is not what that idea describes. The strongest choice is: The Code also expects professionals to encourage others to practice in a way that reflects credit on the profession.

stem: The handbook discusses recommended procedures firms can adopt. Which statement about those procedures is most accurate?
choices: They are recommended ways to support the Standards. Missing a recommendation is not automatically a violation if the Standard itself was met.
Recommended procedures replace the Standards when a firm writes its own manual.
Every recommended procedure is a Standard, so skipping any recommendation is itself a violation.
explanation: The Standards are the duties. Recommended procedures are practical ways to meet them, and firms can design other reasonable systems. A firm manual does not erase the Standards. The violation question is whether the Standard was breached, not whether every suggested procedure was copied. The strongest choice is: They are recommended ways to support the Standards. Missing a recommendation is not automatically a violation if the Standard itself was met.

stem: How can a Professional Conduct Program inquiry begin through the member’s own paperwork?
choices: The member posts a product advertisement that mentions the charter.
The member pays annual dues without writing anything else.
The member discloses the matter on the annual Professional Conduct Statement.
explanation: Self-disclosure on the Professional Conduct Statement is a designed starting point for the program. An advertisement or a dues payment is not that disclosure. The statement is where members are asked to report matters the program should know about. The strongest choice is: The member discloses the matter on the annual Professional Conduct Statement.

stem: A client writes to CFA Institute describing conduct by a charterholder that the client believes broke the Standards. What is the most accurate description of that letter?
choices: Only a court judgment can start an inquiry, so a client letter is discarded.
A written complaint can start a Professional Conduct Program inquiry.
Complaints are accepted only from other CFA charterholders.
explanation: The program accepts written complaints and does not limit complainants to charterholders. A letter is not a finding of a violation. It is a way an inquiry can begin, alongside self-disclosure and information from public sources. The strongest choice is: A written complaint can start a Professional Conduct Program inquiry.

stem: A newspaper reports that a regulator fined a charterholder for falsifying client statements. No one has complained to CFA Institute. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The program may open a file only when the member confesses in writing.
Public information about professional misconduct can prompt a Professional Conduct Program inquiry.
News of a regulatory fine is irrelevant because the program ignores outside authorities.
explanation: The program can learn of possible misconduct from public sources, including regulatory actions reported in the press. It does not need to wait for a confession. A news report still has to be investigated; it is not itself a sanction. The strongest choice is: Public information about professional misconduct can prompt a Professional Conduct Program inquiry.

stem: After an inquiry opens, which description of the process is most accurate?
choices: Staff, led by a designated officer, investigate, and the member has a chance to respond before any sanction is imposed.
A hearing is required before anyone even reads the complaint.
The member is sanctioned on the day the complaint arrives, with no investigation.
explanation: An inquiry is not a conviction. The designated officer’s process gathers information and gives the member an opportunity to respond. A hearing comes later only if the matter proceeds and the member contests a proposed sanction. The strongest choice is: Staff, led by a designated officer, investigate, and the member has a chance to respond before any sanction is imposed.

stem: The designated officer proposes a sanction and the member agrees to it. Which outcome fits the process?
choices: Acceptance is ignored, and every case must still be tried in a public court.
Acceptance automatically upgrades the sanction to revocation.
The member can accept the proposed sanction, and a hearing is not required.
explanation: The process allows a member to accept a proposed sanction and end the matter without a hearing panel. Acceptance does not, by itself, increase the sanction. The program is not required to move every file into a court. The strongest choice is: The member can accept the proposed sanction, and a hearing is not required.

stem: A member rejects a sanction proposed by the designated officer. Who hears the matter under the Professional Conduct Program?
choices: The team that writes CFA exam questions.
The member’s current employer, sitting as the final authority.
A hearing panel drawn from the Disciplinary Review Committee.
explanation: If the member does not accept the proposed sanction, the case goes to a hearing panel of the Disciplinary Review Committee, a volunteer body of charterholders involved in enforcement. Exam writers and the employer are not that panel. The strongest choice is: A hearing panel drawn from the Disciplinary Review Committee.

stem: Which list best names disciplinary sanctions the Professional Conduct Program can impose on a member?
choices: Only a private verbal reminder, with no effect on membership or the designation.
A fine payable to the client, set by the exam grading team.
Public censure, suspension of membership and of the right to use the designation, and revocation.
explanation: Sanctions go beyond a hallway reminder. They include public censure, a timed suspension of membership and of the right to use the designation, and revocation. Exam graders do not invoice clients as the program’s sanction. The strongest choice is: Public censure, suspension of membership and of the right to use the designation, and revocation.

stem: A candidate who has not earned the charter cheats on an exam and the misconduct is established. Which outcome is available?
choices: The candidate can be suspended or barred from further participation in the CFA Program.
Candidates are outside the program, so no professional-conduct consequence exists.
The only available step is to award the charter with a warning footnote.
explanation: Candidates are inside the conduct system. Established cheating can bring suspension or a bar from the program. It does not result in awarding the charter. Membership sanctions such as revocation apply to members; candidates face program sanctions suited to their status. The strongest choice is: The candidate can be suspended or barred from further participation in the CFA Program.

stem: The designated officer issues a cautionary letter and does not propose censure, suspension, or revocation. Which description is most accurate?
choices: A cautionary letter is a possible result of an inquiry and is not the same thing as revocation of membership.
A cautionary letter is issued only by a criminal court.
A cautionary letter automatically revokes the designation.
explanation: Not every inquiry ends in a public disciplinary sanction. A cautionary letter warns the member without being revocation. It is part of the professional-conduct process, not a criminal sentence. The strongest choice is: A cautionary letter is a possible result of an inquiry and is not the same thing as revocation of membership.

stem: What is the Disciplinary Review Committee’s role relative to the Professional Conduct Program?
choices: It is the volunteer committee of charterholders that provides the hearing panels for contested enforcement matters.
It certifies investment firms that claim compliance with performance-reporting rules.
It writes the curriculum readings and grades the exams.
explanation: The Disciplinary Review Committee is an enforcement body in the conduct process. It is not the exam-writing function, and it does not certify firms. Firm performance claims are a separate topic from a member’s disciplinary hearing. The strongest choice is: It is the volunteer committee of charterholders that provides the hearing panels for contested enforcement matters.

stem: A member resigns after a Professional Conduct Program inquiry has already opened into conduct that occurred while she was a member. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Resignation deletes the inquiry and restores the designation automatically.
Resignation transfers the inquiry to the member’s new employer to decide.
Ending membership does not, by itself, stop review of conduct that occurred while she was a member.
explanation: The conduct system is not a club the member can exit in order to erase a file that is already open. Resignation is not an acquittal and does not hand the decision to a new employer. The strongest choice is: Ending membership does not, by itself, stop review of conduct that occurred while she was a member.

stem: A client asks CFA Institute to “revoke the firm” because one employee, who is a charterholder, falsified a report. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The program’s ordinary sanction is to close the firm and seize its client accounts.
Only firms, never individuals, can be censured under the program.
The Professional Conduct Program disciplines members and candidates, not business entities as if the firm held the charter.
explanation: The charter and membership belong to people. Sanctions such as censure, suspension, and revocation run against the member or, for candidates, against participation in the program. The program is not a regulator that shuts a firm down. The strongest choice is: The Professional Conduct Program disciplines members and candidates, not business entities as if the firm held the charter.

stem: Which statement about the scope of the Code and Standards is most accurate?
choices: They apply only while a person is sitting for an exam.
They apply only to equity research and not to wealth management.
They cover professional conduct, and some personal conduct can matter when it reflects on honesty or fitness for the work.
explanation: The duties are professional duties, and they are not limited to exam week or to one product line. Personal dishonesty can still fall inside the conduct system when it undermines fitness for a role clients must trust. The strongest choice is: They cover professional conduct, and some personal conduct can matter when it reflects on honesty or fitness for the work.

stem: A member learns the Standards and ignores the Code, calling the Code “too general to matter.” Which correction is most accurate?
choices: The Code’s broad ideas are still obligations. The Standards specify conduct; they do not retire the Code.
A member may elect either the Code or the Standards, but not both.
The Code is marketing language and cannot sit beside the Standards.
explanation: The Code and the Standards work together. Breadth is not the same thing as being optional. A member does not get to keep the specific rules and discard the principles those rules express, including client priority, independent judgment, and competence. The strongest choice is: The Code’s broad ideas are still obligations. The Standards specify conduct; they do not retire the Code.

stem: Nadia Okonkwo manages portfolios from Piper Street Capital’s office in a country that requires written supervisory pre-approval before any personal trade. The Code and Standards do not prescribe that specific form. Nadia skips the form and says, “The Standards never mention it.” Which standard did Nadia most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
Standard V(C) Record Retention
explanation: Nadia broke a local rule that is stricter than the Code and Standards. That is a violation of Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, which requires the stricter of applicable law and the Code and Standards. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions is a weaker fit because the vignette does not show her trading ahead of clients. Standard V(C) Record Retention is a weaker fit because the missing piece is a legally required approval, not the seven-year research file. The strongest choice is: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law

stem: Mei Chen, an operations analyst at Harbor Glass, is told to prepare invoices that relabel client custody cash as firm revenue. She knows the relabeling is illegal. She emails her manager “I have concerns,” then submits the invoices for the next three months when nobody replies. Which standard did Mei most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(D) Misconduct
Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law
explanation: Mei knew the invoices were unlawful and kept preparing them. Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law requires her to dissociate from illegal activity, not merely to send one note and continue. Standard I(D) Misconduct is a weaker fit because the facts center on continued participation in a known legal breach, not on a separate personal fraud she invented. Standard IV(A) Loyalty is a weaker fit because loyalty to Harbor Glass does not require her to keep filing illegal invoices. The strongest choice is: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law

stem: Owen Blake covers public pensions for Westmill Fund. His home-office gift policy allows a bottle of wine under fifty dollars. The country where the pension officers work sets the gift limit at zero and treats any gift as a prohibited inducement. Owen delivers a forty-dollar bottle to an officer who is reviewing Westmill’s mandate. Which standard did Owen most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard III(C) Suitability
explanation: The host-country ban is stricter than both the firm’s fifty-dollar custom and any looser reading of the Code and Standards. Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law requires Owen to follow that stricter law. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because this gift was given by the adviser, not accepted by Owen as an inducement to change his research. Standard III(C) Suitability is a weaker fit because no client portfolio or IPS is at issue. The strongest choice is: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law

stem: Prospects of Lowcountry Bank live in a province that forbids cold calls to people on a do-not-call list. Luis Ortega’s previous office, in another province, allowed those calls if the banker had once collected a business card. Luis calls three listed prospects from the new province and cites the old rule. Which standard did Luis most likely violate?
choices: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law
Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
explanation: Luis applied the looser rule of a different province and broke the law that actually governs the prospects. Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law makes the stricter applicable law the one he must follow. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is a weaker fit because the problem is the illegal contact method, not a failure to separate fact from opinion or to disclose fees. Standard III(B) Fair Dealing is a weaker fit because he did not favor one existing client over another with a recommendation. The strongest choice is: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law

stem: Local regulations require Piper Street Capital to keep client-recommendation files for ten years. The Code and Standards use seven years only when no stricter rule applies. Which action by Amina Shah is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Delete the files at seven years because that figure appears in the Standards.
Keep the files for three years to save storage unless a client asks for a longer hold.
Archive the recommendation files for ten years because the local rule is stricter.
explanation: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law requires Amina to follow the stricter of local law and the Code and Standards. A ten-year legal hold is stricter than the seven-year default, so the ten-year archive complies. Deleting at seven years, or at three, participates in a breach of the stricter law. The other two actions treat a default, or convenience, as permission to undercut the statute. The strongest choice is: Archive the recommendation files for ten years because the local rule is stricter.

stem: Elena Vasquez is drafting an initiation report on Northline Foods. The investor-relations officer offers her three nights at a private vineyard, including a cooking class that is unrelated to the plant tour. Elena accepts and pays for none of the vineyard stay. Which standard did Elena most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
explanation: The vineyard stay is lavish entertainment with no real business purpose, offered by the issuer while Elena is initiating coverage. That threatens Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because the facts do not show a false statement, plagiarism, or a guaranteed return. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation is a weaker fit because no performance number was published. The strongest choice is: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity

stem: Quill Software offers Harbor Glass 40,000 dollars for a research report and will pay only if the published rating is “outperform” or better. Patrick Nguyen agrees to that payment term before he finishes the model. Which standard did Patrick most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
explanation: Tying the issuer’s fee to a favorable rating lets the subject of the research buy the conclusion. That is a violation of Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis is a weaker fit because the vignette’s defect is the contingent fee, not a missing filing review. Standard VI(C) Referral Fees is a weaker fit because nobody referred a client; the issuer is paying for a rating. The strongest choice is: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity

stem: Piper Street Capital’s equity-capital-markets desk asks Jonah Ellis to lift his “sell” on Lumen Rail to “hold” until a secondary offering closes. Jonah’s model is unchanged. That afternoon he changes only the rating label. Which standard did Jonah most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
explanation: Jonah bent a published opinion to suit his firm’s corporate-finance timetable. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is the best fit because the pressure came from the deal team and the rating moved without a new view. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis is a weaker fit because he already had a completed model; the failure was overriding it for the offering. Standard IV(A) Loyalty is a weaker fit because loyalty to the employer does not mean retuning research to protect a fee. The strongest choice is: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity

stem: A broker offers Mei Chen, who votes Westmill Fund’s approved-broker list, box seats at a championship game worth about 8,000 dollars if her vote moves that broker to the top of the list. Execution quality among the finalists is similar. Mei accepts the seats and changes her vote. Which standard did Mei most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
explanation: The seats are lavish and explicitly tied to Mei’s broker vote, so Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is the best fit. Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care would be stronger if the facts showed worse prices or a research benefit that failed the client. Here execution quality is similar and the problem is the inducement. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is a weaker fit because she did not fake volume or spread a false rumor. The strongest choice is: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity

stem: Iris Media will pay a flat 12,000 dollars for a research report. The fee does not depend on the rating, Iris Media cannot edit the conclusion, and the first page will say that the issuer paid for the report and did not control it. Which action by Diego Martins is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Allow Iris Media to delete two negative paragraphs because it paid for the project.
Add a success fee that is owed only if the shares rise 10 percent after publication.
Publish the report on those terms, with the payment and the lack of issuer control stated on the first page.
explanation: Issuer-paid research can be consistent with Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity when the fee is flat, the issuer cannot shape the conclusion, and the arrangement is disclosed. Letting Iris Media delete criticism, or adding a fee that depends on a rising price, gives the issuer the outcome it paid to control. Those two actions are worse because they sell the opinion. The strongest choice is: Publish the report on those terms, with the payment and the lack of issuer control stated on the first page.

stem: Diego Martins copies the competitive-analysis section of a regional broker’s note into a Westmill Fund report, changes the font, and adds no citation. Which standard did Diego most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
explanation: Using another analyst’s write-up without attribution is plagiarism. That violates Standard I(C) Misrepresentation. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because nobody offered a gift or tied a fee to the rating. Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program is a weaker fit because the report does not misuse the charter or claim a CFA Institute certification. The strongest choice is: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation

stem: Grace Adeyemi shows prospects a slide titled “Live results, 2014–2025” for a strategy that launched last year. Ten of the twelve years are backtests. The footnote never says the earlier years are simulated. Which standard did Grace most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
explanation: Presenting simulated years as live results omits a material fact about what the numbers are. That is a violation of Standard I(C) Misrepresentation. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation is a weaker fit because the distinctive defect is the undisclosed simulation, not a cherry-picked list of real accounts. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because she did not trade on or tip nonpublic information. The strongest choice is: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation

stem: Samuel Iqbal tells a prospect at Piper Street Capital, “If you hire us, your account will not fall more than 2 percent in any quarter.” He believes the hedge will work. Which standard did Samuel most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard I(E) Competence
Standard III(C) Suitability
explanation: A promise that losses cannot exceed a stated amount guarantees performance. That violates Standard I(C) Misrepresentation even when the speaker is sincere. Standard I(E) Competence is a weaker fit because the vignette does not show that Samuel lacks skill; it shows an assurance he cannot honestly give. Standard III(C) Suitability is a weaker fit because no IPS comparison has been made; the sentence itself is the problem. The strongest choice is: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation

stem: Hannah Brooks’s proposal for a Harbor Glass model says the past figures are “our audited client performance.” The figures are hypothetical index returns, and no client account was audited. Which standard did Hannah most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
Standard V(C) Record Retention
explanation: Calling hypothetical index returns audited client performance is a false description of the record. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is the best fit. Standard V(C) Record Retention is a weaker fit because the issue is what she told the prospect, not how long files were kept. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts is a weaker fit because the facts do not describe an ownership or board conflict. The strongest choice is: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation

stem: Leah Bernstein wants to show how a screen would have behaved. She uses index data from a vendor she names, and the chart heading reads “Hypothetical illustration, not the record of an actual account.” Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Use the chart with the vendor citation and the hypothetical heading.
Retitle the chart “Audited client track record” so the sales meeting moves faster.
Paste a rival firm’s commentary under the chart and remove the rival’s name.
explanation: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is met when simulated or hypothetical results are labeled as such and someone else’s work is not presented as her own. The vendor citation and the heading do that. Retitling the chart as an audited client record, or stripping a rival’s name from copied commentary, misstates what the audience is seeing. The strongest choice is: Use the chart with the vendor citation and the hypothetical heading.

stem: Luis Ortega submits a 1,840-dollar dinner receipt to Westmill Fund for a “client meeting” with Lumen Rail. The dinner was his wedding anniversary, and no client attended. Which standard did Luis most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
Standard I(D) Misconduct
explanation: A fabricated expense claim is an act of dishonesty that reflects on trustworthiness. That violates Standard I(D) Misconduct. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because an issuer did not give him the dinner to sway research. Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements is a weaker fit because this is a false claim against his employer, not outside pay he failed to clear in writing. The strongest choice is: Standard I(D) Misconduct

stem: Ruth Abebe already bought shares in her personal account. She then forges her supervisor’s initials on the personal-trade pre-clearance form so the file looks timely. Which standard did Ruth most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors
Standard I(D) Misconduct
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
explanation: Forging the initials is deceit aimed at a control record. Standard I(D) Misconduct is the best fit. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions would be stronger if the facts showed her trading ahead of clients; the vignette centers on the forged approval. Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors is a weaker fit because Ruth is not the supervisor who failed to build a system. The strongest choice is: Standard I(D) Misconduct

stem: Yusuf Demir, a portfolio manager in Lowcountry Bank’s trust department, is convicted of filing a false insurance claim for flood damage to a car that was never damaged. The claim was personal and did not involve client accounts. Which standard did Yusuf most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
Standard I(D) Misconduct
Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
explanation: Fraud outside the portfolio still reflects adversely on honesty and fitness for a role clients must trust. That is Standard I(D) Misconduct. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because he did not misstate investment performance, credentials, or a model. Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care is a weaker fit because no client asset was mismanaged in the vignette. The strongest choice is: Standard I(D) Misconduct

stem: After a client leaves Clara Mendes’s office, Clara changes the risk score on the client’s signed questionnaire so the file appears eligible for a concentrated private fund the client had wanted. Which standard did Clara most likely violate?
choices: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard I(D) Misconduct
explanation: Altering a signed questionnaire is dishonest conduct. Standard I(D) Misconduct is the best fit. Standard III(C) Suitability is related, because the true score may make the fund unsuitable, but the act being judged is the alteration of the client’s record. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is a weaker fit because she did not merely omit a risk discussion; she falsified the form. The strongest choice is: Standard I(D) Misconduct

stem: A client account at Northline Foods’ pension falls 18 percent after a recommendation Ingrid Solberg had researched and documented. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Rewrite last quarter’s memo so it appears she predicted this exact drop.
Ask operations to move the account off her name before the quarter-end report is printed.
Leave the performance records unchanged and explain the loss to the client.
explanation: A bad outcome alone is not misconduct. Standard I(D) Misconduct reaches dishonesty, fraud, and conduct that reflects adversely on trustworthiness, not a researched loss honestly reported. Rewriting the memo or moving the account before the report would be deceitful responses to the same loss, and those actions are worse. The strongest choice is: Leave the performance records unchanged and explain the loss to the client.

stem: Fatima Noor, an equity generalist at Harbor Glass, agrees the same week to run a portfolio of catastrophe bonds. She cannot describe an attachment point or the peril model, and she does not consult anyone who can. Which standard did Fatima most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard I(E) Competence
Standard I(D) Misconduct
explanation: Fatima took a mandate she is not competent to run and did not close that gap. That violates Standard I(E) Competence. Standard I(D) Misconduct is a weaker fit because the facts show a skill failure, not fraud or a forged record. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is a weaker fit because she did not spread a rumor or create false trading activity. The strongest choice is: Standard I(E) Competence

stem: Nicole Hart signs a Harbor Glass note on a bank capital instrument written by an intern from a template Nicole has never read. She cannot explain the coupon reset and signs because the intern “sounded confident.” Which standard did Nicole most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(E) Competence
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
explanation: Nicole held out work she cannot understand as her own professional product. Standard I(E) Competence is the best fit because she lacked the competence the role required and did not maintain it before signing. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis overlaps, but the vignette stresses that she is unable to explain the instrument at all, not merely that one data point was stale. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because she did not plagiarize or guarantee a return. The strongest choice is: Standard I(E) Competence

stem: The money-market rule in Owen Blake’s market changed this year. Owen has not read it. He still tells clients that a fund he recommends “cannot break a dollar” under the old rule, which no longer exists. Which standard did Owen most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(E) Competence
Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
explanation: Owen kept advising on a product after he failed to maintain competence in the rules that govern it. Standard I(E) Competence is the best fit. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a possible cousin because the sentence is outdated, yet the facts emphasize that he did not keep his knowledge current. Standard III(C) Suitability is a weaker fit because the vignette does not compare the fund with a client’s IPS. The strongest choice is: Standard I(E) Competence

stem: Victor Lang accepts a side mandate to trade single-name credit default swaps, a product he has never used. That afternoon he emails a buy recommendation based on a podcast. Which standard did Victor most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(E) Competence
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
explanation: Victor recommended a product he is not competent to handle and did nothing to become competent first. That violates Standard I(E) Competence. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because the podcast is not described as material nonpublic information. Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs is a weaker fit because no exam content was shared and no one cheated. The strongest choice is: Standard I(E) Competence

stem: A client asks Ingrid Solberg to add a cryptocurrency-futures sleeve. She has never traded that market. No rule in the Standards names a required continuing-education course. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Refuse on the ground that the Standards mandate a specific CFA Institute crypto course she has not completed.
Decline to run the sleeve until she has learned the market or paired with a specialist who has.
Accept the sleeve today because a later loss would not, by itself, prove incompetence.
explanation: Standard I(E) Competence requires her to act with competence and to maintain it. It does not treat a bad outcome as automatic incompetence, and it does not mandate a named course. Declining or adding a specialist meets the duty. Accepting immediately misuses the “bad outcome” point. Inventing a required CFA Institute course misstates the Standard. The strongest choice is: Decline to run the sleeve until she has learned the market or paired with a specialist who has.

stem: In an elevator, Lumen Rail’s CFO tells Amina Shah, “Tomorrow’s release will show a covenant breach.” Before the release, Amina buys put options in client accounts she manages at Piper Street Capital. Which standard did Amina most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
explanation: The covenant breach is material and not yet public, and Amina traded on it. That violates Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is a weaker fit because she did not create a false price or a fake rumor; she traded on real undisclosed news. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis is a weaker fit because the failure is the source of the information, not a thin model. The strongest choice is: Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

stem: Henrik Dahl’s former roommate represents the bidder in a deal and tells Henrik that Quill Software will announce a cash offer at 48 dollars on Thursday. On Wednesday Henrik buys Quill shares for the Westmill Fund portfolio he manages. Which standard did Henrik most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
explanation: A pending offer price from the bidder’s lawyer is material and nonpublic. Trading on it violates Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because the roommate did not pay for a research opinion. Standard VI(C) Referral Fees is a weaker fit because no client was referred and no referral fee was paid. The strongest choice is: Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

stem: During a closed board session, Sofia Alvarez learns that Iris Media will cut its dividend that night. She texts her cousin, “Sell Iris before the close.” Sofia does not sell her own shares. Which standard did Sofia most likely violate?
choices: Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
explanation: Tipping material nonpublic information is enough; Sofia did not need to trade herself. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits the tip. Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality is a weaker fit because the information is issuer-board information, not a client’s confidential holdings, and the wrong is the tip for trading. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions is a weaker fit because the cousin’s sale is not an order placed ahead of Sofia’s clients in her firm’s book. The strongest choice is: Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

stem: A print shop Westmill Fund uses hands Marcus Hale a still-embargoed copy of Northline Foods’ earnings release showing a 30 percent profit drop. An hour before the wire, Marcus sells the stock in the fund. Which standard did Marcus most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
explanation: The embargoed release is material and nonpublic, whatever the paper it is printed on. Selling ahead of the wire violates Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because Marcus did not publish a false statement. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation is a weaker fit because no performance composite was shown. The strongest choice is: Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

stem: Leah Bernstein’s buy decision on Lowcountry Bank uses public call reports, branch visits that recorded only foot traffic anyone on the sidewalk could see, and an industry default study. None of the inputs is material nonpublic information. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Call the treasurer, learn the unaudited quarterly loss, and buy before the filing.
Also trade after a director whispers the unpublished merger price, and call the whisper part of the mosaic.
Buy the bonds on that mosaic.
explanation: Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information allows a conclusion reached from public information and nonmaterial observations. That is the mosaic Leah used. Adding a whispered merger price, or an unaudited loss that is not public, brings material nonpublic information into the decision, and those trades are worse. The strongest choice is: Buy the bonds on that mosaic.

stem: Jillian Crowe’s fund is short Lumen Rail. She posts in a trader chat that she “has a letter showing Lumen Rail failed its brake test.” She knows there is no letter. Which standard did Jillian most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
explanation: Inventing a safety failure to push a price while she is short is a false rumor used to move the market. That violates Standard II(B) Market Manipulation. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because the letter does not exist, so she is not trading on real nonpublic news. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because the statement is aimed at the market price, not at a client report or a credential. The strongest choice is: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation

stem: Omar Farouk places simultaneous buy and sell orders of 50,000 shares in a thinly traded Iris Media listing, using two accounts he controls. His only aim is to print volume so the shares look active. Which standard did Omar most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
explanation: Offsetting orders that are intended only to fake activity are wash trades. That violates Standard II(B) Market Manipulation. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions is a weaker fit because he is not jumping a queue ahead of clients; both sides are his. Standard III(B) Fair Dealing is a weaker fit because no client recommendation was withheld from some clients and given to others. The strongest choice is: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation

stem: Patrick Nguyen’s fee is calculated from the quarter-end price of a small holding. In the last two minutes of the quarter he buys 8,000 shares solely to lift that print, then sells them the next morning. Which standard did Patrick most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
explanation: Trading only to set the mark that drives his fee distorts the price. That violates Standard II(B) Market Manipulation. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation would be stronger if he had misstated a return in a slide. Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care is a weaker fit because the vignette’s mechanism is the artificial print, not a soft-dollar purchase or a careless broker choice. The strongest choice is: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation

stem: Elena Vasquez owns call options on Quill Software. She posts a fabricated screenshot of a “Harbor Glass upgrade” of Quill. Harbor Glass has published no such report. Which standard did Elena most likely violate?
choices: Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
explanation: A fake upgrade circulated to move a stock she holds is market manipulation. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is the best fit. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because no issuer or banker pressured a real research opinion. Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program is a weaker fit because the fake document is a research upgrade, not a claim about the charter or about CFA Institute certifying a firm. The strongest choice is: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation

stem: A pension client must raise cash for a benefit payment. Diego Martins sells 1.2 million shares of Northline Foods through a working order. The sale is real, and he spreads no story about the company. The price falls 4 percent. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Cross the block between two of his books at a prearranged price away from the market to set a benchmark.
Also email reporters a false rumor so the remaining shares can be bought back cheaper.
Complete the genuine sale through the normal trading process.
explanation: A large real order can move the price and still be legitimate. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is not violated by that sale. Adding a false rumor, or printing a prearranged cross to manufacture a benchmark, is trading or publicity aimed at a distorted price, and those actions are worse. The strongest choice is: Complete the genuine sale through the normal trading process.

stem: Grace Adeyemi spends client commission credits, earned on Harbor Glass equity trades, on a 9,000-dollar sofa for the reception area. Which standard did Grace most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
explanation: Soft-dollar benefits must help the client. Furniture for the office does not. That violates Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because the sofa was not a gift from an issuer trying to sway a rating. Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements is a weaker fit because she did not accept outside pay; she misused client brokerage. The strongest choice is: Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care

stem: Two brokers execute Westmill Fund’s names with similar prices. One charges 2 cents a share. Samuel Iqbal sends the orders to his sister’s broker at 8 cents a share so she can make her monthly target. Which standard did Samuel most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
explanation: Directing client trades to a more expensive broker to help a relative fails loyalty and care and does not seek best execution. Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care is the best fit. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because the issue is the client’s execution cost, not Samuel’s research opinion. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions is a weaker fit because he did not trade a personal account ahead of clients. The strongest choice is: Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care

stem: The treasurer who hired Priya Raman asks her to buy the treasurer’s brother’s newly listed stock for a pension whose IPS is a short-duration bond mandate. Priya buys the stock. Which standard did Priya most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
explanation: The beneficiaries, not the hiring treasurer, are the client. Buying an equity the IPS does not allow, to please the person who hired her, violates Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care. Standard III(C) Suitability is close, because the stock does not fit the mandate, but the best fit is loyalty: she served the treasurer’s family over the beneficiaries. Standard IV(A) Loyalty is a weaker fit because that duty runs to her employer, and the employer’s interest is not the duty she abandoned here. The strongest choice is: Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care

stem: Jonah Ellis votes client shares in favor of a merger that increases Piper Street Capital’s investment-banking fee. His own team’s written analysis said the merger hurts the beneficiaries. Which standard did Jonah most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
explanation: Proxy votes are an asset of the client. Using them to protect the firm’s banking fee, against the beneficiaries’ interest, violates Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity would be stronger if a research rating had been rewritten. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is a weaker fit because no false trading or rumor was used. The strongest choice is: Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care

stem: Mei Chen can send client trades to a broker charging 4 cents a share that supplies a credit model her client portfolios actually use, or to a 1-cent broker that supplies no research. She documents the research benefit and reviews execution quality each quarter. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Send every order to the most expensive broker because the salesperson is a friend and provides nothing the clients use.
Use the 4-cent broker, keep the documentation, and continue the execution review.
Spend the commission credits on her own CFA exam registration.
explanation: Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care allows client brokerage to pay for research that benefits the clients when execution remains part of the decision. Mei’s documentation and review fit that duty. Exam fees benefit her, and a friend’s high commission with no client benefit fails best execution. Those two uses are worse. The strongest choice is: Use the 4-cent broker, keep the documentation, and continue the execution review.

stem: Omar Farouk phones Westmill Fund’s three largest clients with a downgrade of Quill Software at 9:10 a.m. He emails the same note to all other clients at 11:00 a.m. Which standard did Omar most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
explanation: A changed recommendation has to reach clients of the same service level fairly. Calling the largest accounts first violates Standard III(B) Fair Dealing. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is a weaker fit because the note’s content is not the defect; the head start is. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because a downgrade he is publishing is not someone else’s nonpublic information he tipped. The strongest choice is: Standard III(B) Fair Dealing

stem: Iris Media’s IPO is three times oversubscribed. Hannah Brooks fills her husband’s fee-paying account in full and prorates every other client. Which standard did Hannah most likely violate?
choices: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
explanation: A hot issue was allocated to a family account ahead of other clients. That violates Standard III(B) Fair Dealing. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions is close if she controls the husband’s trading, but the best fit is the unfair allocation among clients of a scarce new issue. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts is a weaker fit because disclosure of the relationship would not cure a preferential fill. The strongest choice is: Standard III(B) Fair Dealing

stem: Nadia Okonkwo sequences a new buy on Lumen Rail so Piper Street Capital’s proprietary book is filled before any client order. Which standard did Nadia most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
explanation: Trading the house book ahead of clients on a new recommendation withholds the idea from clients. Standard III(B) Fair Dealing is the best fit. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions would be stronger if the early order were her personal or beneficial-family account rather than the firm’s proprietary book versus clients. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is a weaker fit because the orders are real trades in a real view, not a scheme to fake the price. The strongest choice is: Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
