stem: The published menu for Ruth Abebe’s “platinum” tier promises longer meetings and a named contact, not earlier trades. She still gives platinum clients a new recommendation two hours before other advisory clients who pay for the same research. Which standard did Ruth most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
explanation: Different service levels can be acceptable when they are disclosed and actually match the practice. An undisclosed head start on the recommendation violates Standard III(B) Fair Dealing. Standard III(C) Suitability is a weaker fit because the vignette is about timing among clients, not about an IPS. Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements is a weaker fit because no outside paycheck is being accepted. The strongest choice is: Standard III(B) Fair Dealing

stem: Yusuf Demir offers a disclosed execution-only tier and a disclosed full-advisory tier. A recommendation change goes out at the same time to every full-advisory client. Execution-only clients do not receive advice, as their agreements state. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Allocate an oversubscribed new issue only to accounts that are just below a performance-fee high-water mark.
Within the full-advisory tier, call the largest fee payers two hours before the others.
Keep that two-tier schedule and the simultaneous notice to full-advisory clients.
explanation: Standard III(B) Fair Dealing allows different service levels that are disclosed and does not allow favoritism inside a level or hot-issue allocation aimed at fees. Yusuf’s schedule matches the disclosed tiers and treats advisory clients together. Early calls to fee leaders, and allocations designed to switch on performance fees, are worse. The strongest choice is: Keep that two-tier schedule and the simultaneous notice to full-advisory clients.

stem: Clara Mendes places a retiree’s entire 400,000-dollar IRA into a 12-year lockup private-credit fund. The IPS says spending from the IRA starts next year. Which standard did Clara most likely violate?
choices: Standard V(C) Record Retention
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
Standard III(C) Suitability
explanation: A long lockup does not fund spending that starts next year. The recommendation does not fit the IPS, so Standard III(C) Suitability is the best fit. Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care is a weaker fit because the vignette does not show self-dealing or soft-dollar misuse; it shows a mismatch with stated needs. Standard V(C) Record Retention is a weaker fit because no file was destroyed. The strongest choice is: Standard III(C) Suitability

stem: A client tells Luis Ortega he was laid off and must withdraw tuition in four months. Luis leaves the IPS as “long horizon, high risk” and buys more volatile small caps the same day. Which standard did Luis most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(E) Competence
Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
explanation: A job loss and a near-term cash need are material changes. Updating the IPS before adding risk is part of Standard III(C) Suitability. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is a weaker fit because he did not fail to label an opinion or disclose a fee; he ignored new circumstances. Standard I(E) Competence is a weaker fit because the facts do not show he lacks skill. The strongest choice is: Standard III(C) Suitability

stem: Fatima Noor recommends a three-times leveraged inverse equity ETF as the cash sleeve for a client whose IPS limits drawdowns in the liquidity bucket to nearly zero. Which standard did Fatima most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
explanation: The product can move sharply and does not behave like cash. Recommending it for that bucket violates Standard III(C) Suitability. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is a weaker fit because she did not distort a market price. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because the vignette does not quote a false performance claim; it shows an unsuitable product choice. The strongest choice is: Standard III(C) Suitability

stem: A Harbor Glass trust IPS caps any single issuer at 5 percent. Ingrid Solberg, who has discretion, buys a 9 percent position because she has high conviction and does not amend the IPS. Which standard did Ingrid most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
explanation: In a discretionary account the IPS limit is a suitability constraint. Breaching it for conviction violates Standard III(C) Suitability. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis is a weaker fit because the problem is not an empty research file; it is a trade the mandate does not allow. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts is a weaker fit because no personal conflict is described. The strongest choice is: Standard III(C) Suitability

stem: In a non-discretionary account, a client insists on putting 40 percent of the portfolio into one microcap after Elena Vasquez explains that the trade breaks the IPS concentration and liquidity limits. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Refuse every client-directed order she has warned against and freeze the account with no further discussion.
Place the same trade in a discretionary account with the same IPS because the client mentioned the microcap at lunch.
Document the warning and the client’s written direction, then place only that directed order.
explanation: Standard III(C) Suitability still requires the warning and the IPS comparison. In a non-discretionary account, after Elena explains that the trade is unsuitable and the client directs it anyway, she may execute that directed order and should document it. Doing the same trade with discretion, or freezing the account as if discussion were forbidden, is worse. The strongest choice is: Document the warning and the client’s written direction, then place only that directed order.

stem: Victor Lang’s slide “Westmill Small Cap, five years” includes only the 11 accounts that beat the benchmark and leaves out 9 accounts that lagged. Which standard did Victor most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
explanation: Choosing the winners and omitting the losers is a cherry-picked performance picture. That violates Standard III(D) Performance Presentation. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because the accounts shown may be real; the unfairness is the selection, which III(D) specifically addresses. Standard III(B) Fair Dealing is a weaker fit because clients were not given unequal access to a recommendation. The strongest choice is: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation

stem: Amina Shah quotes “18 percent last year” for a strategy and does not say the figure is gross of a 1.40 percent management fee and a 15 percent performance fee. Which standard did Amina most likely violate?
choices: Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
explanation: A performance number that hides the fees it excludes is not a fair and complete presentation. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation is the best fit. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients also cares about costs, but the sentence at issue is a performance claim, so III(D) is the closer duty. Standard VI(C) Referral Fees is a weaker fit because no referral arrangement is described. The strongest choice is: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation

stem: Henrik Dahl removes two accounts that were closed after losses and shows prospects only the accounts that remain. Which standard did Henrik most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard III(C) Suitability
explanation: Terminated accounts still belong in the history of the strategy for the periods they were managed. Dropping them because they lost money violates Standard III(D) Performance Presentation. Standard III(C) Suitability is a weaker fit because no client IPS is being ignored. Standard IV(A) Loyalty is a weaker fit because he did not take models or solicit clients away from an employer. The strongest choice is: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation

stem: Sofia Alvarez compares a short-duration municipal ladder with a small-cap equity index and labels the difference “alpha.” She does not say the benchmark is unrelated to the mandate. Which standard did Sofia most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
explanation: An unmatched benchmark makes the performance comparison misleading. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation is the best fit because the presentation is not fair or complete. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis would be stronger if she had issued a buy recommendation with no research. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because no nonpublic information was used. The strongest choice is: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation

stem: Leah Bernstein’s report includes every account that followed the mandate, keeps terminated accounts in the years they were managed, and shows gross-of-fee and net-of-fee returns beside the fee schedule. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Show only the best year and label it “representative.”
Present gross returns and mention fees only if a prospect asks.
Publish that report as the description of the strategy’s results.
explanation: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation calls for a fair, accurate, and complete picture, including the effect of fees and the accounts that actually followed the strategy. Leah’s report does that. A single “representative” year, or gross returns with fees on request only, leaves out information prospects need. The strongest choice is: Publish that report as the description of the strategy’s results.

stem: At a neighborhood dinner, Marcus Hale names three stocks he bought that week for a well-known novelist who is his client at Piper Street Capital. Which standard did Marcus most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
explanation: The holdings are the client’s confidential information, and dinner-table gossip discloses them. That violates Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because he is not tipping issuer information so someone can trade ahead of a release. Standard III(C) Suitability is a weaker fit because no recommendation or IPS is being judged. The strongest choice is: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality

stem: Jillian Crowe tells a reporter the size and timing of a client’s pending sale of a family business, which she learned in a planning meeting at Lowcountry Bank. Which standard did Jillian most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
explanation: A client’s transaction plans are confidential. Sharing them with a reporter violates Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because she did not publish a false performance or credential claim. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is a weaker fit because the duty breached is silence toward outsiders, not disclosure of risks and fees to the client. The strongest choice is: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality

stem: After leaving Piper Street Capital, Diego Martins uses a printed holdings report he took with him to entertain friends with stories about what each former client owned. Which standard did Diego most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
Standard V(C) Record Retention
explanation: Confidentiality continues after he leaves and covers former clients. Using the holdings as entertainment violates Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality. Standard IV(A) Loyalty is a weaker fit because the stories are not the taking of a model to compete, though taking the report was also wrong; the conduct described is disclosure of holdings. Standard V(C) Record Retention is a weaker fit because the issue is not the seven-year archive. The strongest choice is: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality

stem: A colleague’s spouse asks Grace Adeyemi whether a client is “in trouble with the tax authority.” Grace shares the client’s audit letter. Which standard did Grace most likely violate?
choices: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
Standard I(D) Misconduct
Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
explanation: The audit letter is client information given for the professional relationship. Passing it across a family conversation violates Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality. Standard I(D) Misconduct is a weaker fit because the facts show a confidentiality breach, not a forged document or a fraud conviction. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts is a weaker fit because no beneficial ownership or outside board is involved. The strongest choice is: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality

stem: A CFA Institute Professional Conduct investigator asks Samuel Iqbal for trading records of a former client that are relevant to a written complaint. Local custom is to refuse every outside request. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Provide the records to the Professional Conduct investigator.
Print the same records in a client-appreciation newsletter.
Refuse the investigator on the view that confidentiality is absolute.
explanation: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality does not block cooperation with a CFA Institute Professional Conduct investigation. Providing the relevant records complies. Publishing them in a newsletter is gossip to a different audience. Treating confidentiality as absolute misstates the Standard and is worse. The strongest choice is: Provide the records to the Professional Conduct investigator.

stem: During her two-week notice at Piper Street Capital, Priya Raman emails five clients: “I join Lowcountry Bank on the 1st. Move your accounts so I can keep managing them.” Which standard did Priya most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
explanation: Soliciting clients to follow her while she is still employed violates Standard IV(A) Loyalty. Standard III(B) Fair Dealing is a weaker fit because she did not give some clients an earlier research call. Standard VI(C) Referral Fees is a weaker fit because she did not hide a referral payment; she recruited clients before she left. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(A) Loyalty

stem: The Friday before his resignation, Owen Blake copies Piper Street Capital’s multi-factor spreadsheet and the client-constraint database onto a personal drive. Which standard did Owen most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard V(C) Record Retention
explanation: The model and the client database belong to the firm. Taking them as he leaves violates Standard IV(A) Loyalty. Standard V(C) Record Retention is a weaker fit because the duty to keep records does not make the files his to remove. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because he has not presented the model as a fake track record or as another analyst’s work. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(A) Loyalty

stem: Nicole Hart starts a paid Saturday planning practice for neighbors and earns 600 dollars a month. She never tells Harbor Glass, her full-time employer. Which standard did Nicole most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
explanation: Independent practice that competes with her employer requires consent before she starts. Skipping that consent violates Standard IV(A) Loyalty. Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements is close because outside pay is involved, but the facts are a separate practice opened with no consent, which IV(A) addresses directly. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts is a weaker fit because the missing step is employer consent to the practice, not a disclosure inside a research report. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(A) Loyalty

stem: Ruth Abebe prints Harbor Glass’s pipeline of prospect meeting notes and carries the folder into interviews with a new employer. Which standard did Ruth most likely violate?
choices: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
explanation: Prospect notes assembled by the firm are firm property. Carrying them into a job search violates Standard IV(A) Loyalty. Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality is a weaker fit because the vignette stresses competitive use of the pipeline, not gossip about a client’s holdings. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is a weaker fit because she did not omit risks or fees in a client recommendation. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(A) Loyalty

stem: While employed at Harbor Glass, Mei Chen discovers that the operations manager has been diverting client settlement cash. She has a job offer, and she knows the firm’s valuation layout by heart. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: During her notice period, email clients to follow her and attach the firm’s model as a sample of her work.
Stay silent about the diversion because loyalty to the employer outranks a report, and take the model files so clients are not inconvenienced.
Report the diversion to the regulator, leave the firm’s files and client lists on Harbor Glass systems, and rely on her own skill after she leaves.
explanation: Standard IV(A) Loyalty does not require Mei to conceal a diversion of client cash. Reporting it, leaving the files behind, and using only the skill in her head complies. Silence plus taking the model treats loyalty as cover for misconduct and for removing firm property. Soliciting during the notice period and attaching the model are worse under the same standard. The strongest choice is: Report the diversion to the regulator, leave the firm’s files and client lists on Harbor Glass systems, and rely on her own skill after she leaves.

stem: A client tells Jonah Ellis, “If the account beats the index by 3 percentage points, I will pay you 20,000 dollars personally.” Jonah receives the transfer and tells his boss at Piper Street Capital the next month. Which standard did Jonah most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
explanation: The bonus is outside compensation that can pull him away from his employer’s interest. Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements requires written employer consent before he accepts it. A conversation after the transfer fails that duty. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because the payer is his client, not an issuer buying a rating. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation is a weaker fit because no return was misstated. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements

stem: Iris Media grants Patrick Nguyen options worth about 35,000 dollars a year to advise its treasury. He accepts, attends meetings, and plans to tell Westmill Fund only if someone asks. Which standard did Patrick most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
explanation: The options are compensation from an outside company, accepted with no written consent from his employer. That violates Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts would be the closer fit if he published research on Iris Media without a prominent disclosure. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because the vignette contains no false performance claim, plagiarism, or guaranteed return. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements

stem: A broker pays Hannah Brooks 20 percent of the broker’s commission, personally, for steering a friend’s account to that broker. After the first payment she gets a spoken “sounds fine” from a colleague in a hallway. No written employer consent exists. Which standard did Hannah most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
explanation: Personal pay from the broker is additional compensation. A hallway remark after the payment is not written consent obtained beforehand. That violates Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements. Standard VI(C) Referral Fees is close because a referral is involved, but the person being paid is the member and the missing step in these facts is employer consent. Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care would be stronger if the vignette showed worse execution for existing client orders. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements

stem: Yusuf Demir sits on Quill Software’s advisory board for a 15,000-dollar quarterly stipend. He first mentions the stipend on Westmill Fund’s annual form eight months after the first check. Which standard did Yusuf most likely violate?
choices: Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
explanation: The stipend is outside compensation that creates a conflict with his employer. Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements requires written consent before acceptance, not a form filed months later. Standard IV(A) Loyalty is a weaker fit because he did not solicit clients or remove firm models. Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program is a weaker fit because the board pay does not misuse the charter. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements

stem: A client offers Clara Mendes a 10,000-dollar year-end bonus if her separate account beats the policy benchmark. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Rely on a colleague’s spoken approval and skip written consent because the client already knows about the offer.
Obtain her employer’s written consent describing the payer, the amount, and the conflict, and only then accept the bonus.
Accept the bonus now and file a consent request next quarter.
explanation: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements is satisfied when written employer consent comes first and the conflict is described. Accepting now and paperwork later reverses that order. A colleague’s spoken aside is not the written employer consent the standard requires. Both alternatives are worse. The strongest choice is: Obtain her employer’s written consent describing the payer, the amount, and the conflict, and only then accept the bonus.

stem: Ingrid Solberg supervises Westmill Fund’s traders. She knows the pre-clearance system has been offline for six weeks and that two traders have bought names on the restricted list. She says she will look in the summer. Which standard did Ingrid most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
Standard I(D) Misconduct
explanation: Ingrid knew the control was down and that violations were occurring, and she deferred any response. That violates Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions is a weaker fit because she is not the person who traded ahead of clients. Standard I(D) Misconduct is a weaker fit because the facts show a failure to supervise, not her own forged record or fraud. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors

stem: Victor Lang is named supervisor of a new alternatives desk at Harbor Glass. The desk has no written procedures. He lets the team trade on his first day and does not put procedures in place. Which standard did Victor most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(E) Competence
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors
explanation: Accepting supervision without reasonable procedures, and allowing trading anyway, violates Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis is a weaker fit because the vignette is about the supervisory system, not a single recommendation with no research. Standard I(E) Competence is a weaker fit because the facts do not show he lacks technical skill; they show he supervised without a system. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors

stem: Leah Bernstein sees a subordinate’s email promising a client “no loss of principal.” She deletes her copy and does not speak to the subordinate or to compliance, noting that he hits his numbers. The firm’s manual forbids guarantees. Which standard did Leah most likely violate?
choices: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors
Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
explanation: Once Leah knows of the guarantee, reasonable supervision requires a response. Ignoring it violates Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is the subordinate’s breach, not the best description of the supervisor who saw it and looked away. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is a weaker fit because Leah did not author the client email; she failed to supervise the person who did. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors

stem: Henrik Dahl tells his team to skip the allocation checklist whenever an IPO prices on a Friday, and he does not review those allocations. Which standard did Henrik most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors
Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
explanation: Instructing staff to bypass a control, and then not reviewing the result, is a failure of supervision. Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors is the best fit. Standard III(B) Fair Dealing would be stronger if a particular unfair allocation were the conduct being judged. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is a weaker fit because nobody is described as faking volume or spreading a rumor. The strongest choice is: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors

stem: Omar Farouk trains his team on a written allocation procedure and spot-checks tickets each week. A subordinate still allocates a hot deal to a friend. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Do nothing, because a printed manual means a supervisor is finished once the manual exists.
Escalate the same day, reverse the allocation, and increase reviews of that person.
Stop the weekly spot checks so the manual can “speak for itself.”
explanation: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors is met by a reasonable system that is actually used, plus a prompt response when a breach appears. A subordinate’s violation does not, by itself, mean Omar violated the standard. Ignoring the breach because a manual exists, or dismantling the checks, would make the system unreasonable. Those two actions are worse. The strongest choice is: Escalate the same day, reverse the allocation, and increase reviews of that person.

stem: Sofia Alvarez tells clients to buy Northline Foods because the chief executive’s keynote “felt bullish.” She reads no filing, no industry data, and no financial statement. Which standard did Sofia most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
explanation: A recommendation with no research behind it lacks a reasonable basis. That violates Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because no gift or deal pressure changed a completed opinion. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because she did not present simulated results as real or guarantee a return. The strongest choice is: Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis

stem: A bank publishes a sell report on Lumen Rail. Diego Martins forwards it to every Westmill Fund client as his recommendation within the hour, without reading past the headline. Which standard did Diego most likely violate?
choices: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
explanation: Third-party research can support a recommendation only if the member reviews it. Forwarding an unread headline violates Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because the bank report is published. Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs is a weaker fit because no exam material was shared. The strongest choice is: Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis

stem: Marcus Hale’s model of Quill Software still uses last year’s debt figure after a large bond issue he saw in a press release and ignored. A salesperson asks for a “fresh” note, and Marcus reissues the buy with the old debt that morning. Which standard did Marcus most likely violate?
choices: Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Standard V(C) Record Retention
Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
explanation: Reissuing a recommendation on inputs he knows are stale is not diligence. That violates Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis. Standard V(C) Record Retention is a weaker fit because the file’s age limit is not the defect; the unused new fact is. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation is a weaker fit because he did not publish a performance composite. The strongest choice is: Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis

stem: Jillian Crowe recommends a structured note whose payoff she cannot calculate. The only item in the file is a one-line email from the structurer saying “clients like these.” Which standard did Jillian most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Standard I(E) Competence
explanation: The file has no analysis of how the note pays off. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis is the best fit. Standard I(E) Competence is close if she is unable to understand the product at all; here the emphasis is the empty basis she used for this recommendation. Standard III(C) Suitability is a weaker fit because no client IPS is compared with the note. The strongest choice is: Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis

stem: Samuel Iqbal receives a third-party initiation report on Quill Software. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Raise the price target to the sales desk’s requested number and write a reason the following week.
Forward the third-party PDF to clients the minute it arrives because an outside firm wrote it.
Read the report, check its revenue assumptions against Quill’s public filings, note a disagreement, and only then use it in a client recommendation with his own conclusion.
explanation: Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis allows third-party research when the member reviews it and reaches a conclusion. Samuel’s checks do that. An unread forward has no basis of his own. Changing the target to suit sales and inventing support later abandons the research process. Those two actions are worse. The strongest choice is: Read the report, check its revenue assumptions against Quill’s public filings, note a disagreement, and only then use it in a client recommendation with his own conclusion.

stem: Fatima Noor’s note states, “Lumen Rail will earn 4.20 dollars next year,” as a fact. The figure is her forecast. The note never says it is an opinion and never mentions that a strike at the main yard could erase the earnings. Which standard did Fatima most likely violate?
choices: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
explanation: Clients must be able to tell a forecast from a fact and must hear the risks that matter. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is the best fit. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation would be stronger if she guaranteed a return or hid that results were simulated. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis is a weaker fit because the vignette does not say the forecast lacked research; it says the note presents the forecast badly. The strongest choice is: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients

stem: Piper Street Capital stops using sector analysts and switches the equity process to a pure momentum screen. Amina Shah does not tell existing clients, who still believe analysts are selecting the stocks. Which standard did Amina most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors
explanation: A material change in the investment process has to be communicated. Leaving clients with the old description violates Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients. Standard III(C) Suitability is a weaker fit because no IPS mismatch is described. Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors is a weaker fit because Amina is not failing to supervise a subordinate; she is failing to tell clients about the process. The strongest choice is: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients

stem: Harbor Glass charges a 1.10 percent advisory fee and a separate custody charge of 0.15 percent. Nicole Hart’s new agreements and meetings say only, “We are paid in the normal way,” and never state either figure or that the service is non-discretionary advice. Which standard did Nicole most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
explanation: The nature of the service and the costs to the client are part of what must be disclosed. Vague “normal” pay violates Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients. Standard VI(C) Referral Fees is a weaker fit because no referral arrangement is described. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation is a weaker fit because she did not issue a performance number. The strongest choice is: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients

stem: Owen Blake adds a large high-yield corporate sleeve to a municipal-bond strategy and does not tell clients about the credit risk the change adds. Which standard did Owen most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
explanation: The process and the risk profile changed, and clients were not told. That violates Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because the sleeve is his own portfolio decision, not undisclosed issuer news. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is a weaker fit because he did not fake trading activity. The strongest choice is: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients

stem: Elena Vasquez is onboarding a new Westmill Fund client. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: State that the account is non-discretionary advice, state the 0.75 percent advisory fee and the 50-dollar ticket charge, label her return scenario as an opinion, and list interest-rate and reinvestment risk.
Call the fee “competitive” and present the return scenario as a fact the client can bank on.
Add an options overlay the next quarter and mention it only in a glossary at the back of the tax packet.
explanation: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients covers facts versus opinions, risks, process changes, and the nature of services and costs. Elena’s letter does those things in plain language. Hiding the fee behind “competitive,” stating a scenario as fact, or burying a process change in a tax glossary are worse. The strongest choice is: State that the account is non-discretionary advice, state the 0.75 percent advisory fee and the 50-dollar ticket charge, label her return scenario as an opinion, and list interest-rate and reinvestment risk.

stem: No local rule and no firm manual sets a different period. Grace Adeyemi deletes the models and meeting notes behind a published recommendation after 22 months to clear disk space. Which standard did Grace most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(D) Misconduct
Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
Standard V(C) Record Retention
explanation: With no stricter rule, records that support a recommendation are kept for seven years. Deleting them after 22 months violates Standard V(C) Record Retention. Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality is a weaker fit because she destroyed files rather than gossiping about them. Standard I(D) Misconduct is a weaker fit because the facts show a retention failure, not fraud or a forged client document. The strongest choice is: Standard V(C) Record Retention

stem: When Luis Ortega resigns from Piper Street Capital, he takes the only copies of the files that support his last six buy recommendations, calling them his personal work product. Which standard did Luis most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard V(C) Record Retention
Standard IV(A) Loyalty
explanation: Records supporting recommendations belong to the firm. Removing the only copies violates Standard V(C) Record Retention. Standard IV(A) Loyalty overlaps because taking firm property also breaches loyalty, but the best fit is the record duty: these files exist to support the recommendations and are not his to keep. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because he did not mislabel the work in a client communication. The strongest choice is: Standard V(C) Record Retention

stem: Priya Raman gives a verbal buy recommendation on Iris Media to a prospect and keeps no note of the data, the date, or the risks she described. Which standard did Priya most likely violate?
choices: Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Standard V(C) Record Retention
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
explanation: A recommendation needs a record of its basis even when it is spoken. Keeping nothing violates Standard V(C) Record Retention. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients would be stronger if the facts said she hid risks from the prospect; here the stated failure is the missing record. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis is a weaker fit because the vignette does not say she lacked a basis at the time; it says she kept no record of it. The strongest choice is: Standard V(C) Record Retention

stem: Westmill Fund’s manual requires recommendation files to be kept nine years. Henrik Dahl keeps them seven years and shreds the rest, citing the seven-year figure associated with the Standards. Which standard did Henrik most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law
Standard V(C) Record Retention
explanation: The seven-year period applies only when no stricter local or firm rule exists. The firm’s nine-year manual is stricter, so shredding at seven years violates Standard V(C) Record Retention. Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law is close if a statute had set the longer period; here the stricter rule is the firm manual on the records themselves, so V(C) is the better fit. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation is a weaker fit because no performance exhibit was altered. The strongest choice is: Standard V(C) Record Retention

stem: No stricter local law or firm rule applies to Ruth Abebe’s files at Westmill Fund. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Keep the only copy on her personal laptop and refuse to give the firm a duplicate.
Delete the files after four years because no client has complained.
Store the inputs, the published note, and the client communication on the firm’s archive for seven years, and leave them there when she changes teams.
explanation: Standard V(C) Record Retention sets seven years as the default and treats the records as the firm’s. Ruth’s archive meets both points. A personal-only copy denies the firm its records. Deleting at four years cuts the default short. Those two actions are worse. The strongest choice is: Store the inputs, the published note, and the client communication on the firm’s archive for seven years, and leave them there when she changes teams.

stem: Jonah Ellis is a paid director of Quill Software and publishes a Westmill Fund buy recommendation on Quill. The report never mentions the directorship. Which standard did Jonah most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
explanation: The board seat is a conflict with the published buy. He did not avoid it and did not disclose it. That violates Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts. Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements would be stronger if the facts focused on missing written consent for the director’s pay. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because the vignette does not show the issuer editing his rating; it shows an undisclosed conflict. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts

stem: Mei Chen’s spouse owns 18 percent of a private supplier that benefits if Iris Media wins a contract. Mei recommends Iris Media to clients and does not mention the stake. Which standard did Mei most likely violate?
choices: Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
explanation: The spouse’s stake is a beneficial interest that conflicts with the recommendation. Saying nothing violates Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions is a weaker fit because no personal or family order jumped ahead of clients. Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality is a weaker fit because the missing act is disclosure of a conflict, not protection of a client secret. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts

stem: Harbor Glass has three other food analysts. Nadia Okonkwo’s parents control Northline Foods. She keeps the Northline coverage herself and puts one sentence about the family block in footnote 14 on page 20. Which standard did Nadia most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
explanation: Avoidance was reasonable because other analysts could cover the stock. A buried footnote is not what Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts requires when the conflict can be avoided, and it is not prominent plain language when disclosure is the fallback. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because she did not falsify results. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation is a weaker fit because no performance record was shown. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts

stem: Two private funds are equally suitable for a client mandate. One pays Patrick Nguyen a personal introduction fee. He allocates the client to that fund and never mentions the fee. Which standard did Patrick most likely violate?
choices: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
explanation: He could have avoided the conflict by using the similar fund, and he did not disclose the fee in plain language. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts is the best fit. Standard VI(C) Referral Fees is close if the fee is viewed as a referral, but the facts emphasize his undisclosed beneficial conflict in the allocation decision. Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care is a weaker fit because suitability is equal and the distinctive wrong is the hidden personal fee. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts

stem: Lowcountry Bank has only one transportation analyst, Yusuf Demir. He owns 200 shares of Lumen Rail from years ago, and no other analyst can take the name this month. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Omit the shares because 200 is too small to mention.
State in the first paragraph, in plain language, that he owns 200 shares of Lumen Rail, and document why another analyst could not cover it.
Write in the headline that the note is free of conflicts, and mention the shares only in the data appendix.
explanation: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts says to avoid a conflict when that is reasonable and otherwise to disclose it prominently in plain language. With no other analyst available, prominent disclosure and a written reason fit. Silence, or a “no conflicts” headline with an appendix mention, hides the interest. Those actions are worse. The strongest choice is: State in the first paragraph, in plain language, that he owns 200 shares of Lumen Rail, and document why another analyst could not cover it.

stem: Before entering a large client buy of Quill Software, Clara Mendes buys 3,000 shares in her personal account at 10:02 a.m. Client orders go in at 10:40 a.m. Which standard did Clara most likely violate?
choices: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
explanation: Buying for herself first, ahead of the client order she is about to send, is front-running. That violates Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because the vignette does not say she holds issuer secrets; she is trading ahead of her own client order. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is a weaker fit because the orders are real purchases, not a wash or a rumor. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions

stem: Hannah Brooks controls trading in her husband’s account. In an oversubscribed IPO she fills that account in full and gives client accounts only what remains. Which standard did Hannah most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(A) Loyalty
Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
explanation: A beneficial family account traded ahead of clients in a limited deal. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions is the best fit. Standard III(B) Fair Dealing is close because other clients were shorted, but the early fill is her beneficial account, which is the priority-of-transactions problem. Standard IV(A) Loyalty is a weaker fit because she did not take firm property or solicit clients away. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions

stem: A block of Lumen Rail fills only 60 percent. Victor Lang gives his personal account the full size he requested and prorates client accounts for the rest. Which standard did Victor most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
explanation: Partial fills go to clients before the manager’s own account. Taking a full personal fill first violates Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions. Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care is a weaker fit because the mechanism is trade priority, not soft dollars or a careless broker. Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors is a weaker fit because Victor is allocating his own order, not failing to supervise someone else. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions

stem: Client accounts and Westmill Fund’s house account are both scheduled to buy Iris Media. Ingrid Solberg first buys in her mother’s account, which Ingrid controls, then the house account, then the clients. Which standard did Ingrid most likely violate?
choices: Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions
Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
explanation: The mother’s account is a beneficial trade Ingrid controls. Putting it ahead of clients and the employer violates Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions. Standard III(B) Fair Dealing would be stronger if she had favored one client over other clients with a recommendation. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because no nonpublic issuer information is described. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions

stem: Client orders and Piper Street Capital’s house account in Northline Foods are complete. Samuel Iqbal has the firm’s required pre-clearance. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Trade his minor child’s account in front of clients because the child is not a firm client.
Buy a small personal lot the next day.
Buy the personal lot first on the theory that a small order cannot move the price.
explanation: Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions puts clients and the employer ahead of personal and beneficial-family trades. Trading after those orders are done, with pre-clearance, complies. Trading first because the order is small, or using a child’s account he controls as a workaround, still puts a beneficial trade ahead of clients. Those actions are worse. The strongest choice is: Buy a small personal lot the next day.

stem: Luis Ortega pays an accountant 25 percent of the first-year advisory fee for each client the accountant refers. He tells Harbor Glass in writing and does not tell the prospects. Which standard did Luis most likely violate?
choices: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
explanation: Referral compensation must be disclosed to the client or prospect, not only to the employer. Luis violated Standard VI(C) Referral Fees. Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements is a weaker fit because the payment is his outflow to the accountant, and the employer was told; the missing disclosure is to the prospect. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts is broader, but the specific undisclosed item is a referral fee, so VI(C) is the better fit. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(C) Referral Fees

stem: A custodian pays Fatima Noor 2,000 dollars for every client who transfers a portfolio in. She never mentions the payment to those clients. Which standard did Fatima most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
explanation: A benefit for sending clients to the custodian is a referral fee. Hiding it from the clients violates Standard VI(C) Referral Fees. Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care is a weaker fit because the vignette does not show poor execution or soft-dollar misuse. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because she did not publish a false track record; she omitted the referral arrangement. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(C) Referral Fees

stem: Diego Martins discloses a referral fee in one clause on page 37 of an appendix, and he shows that page only after the client has signed and wired cash. Which standard did Diego most likely violate?
choices: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
explanation: Referral-fee disclosure has to reach the prospect in a way that can affect the decision, not after the wire in a buried clause. That violates Standard VI(C) Referral Fees. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is a weaker fit because the hidden item is specifically referral compensation. Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality is a weaker fit because he did not reveal a client confidence. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(C) Referral Fees

stem: Owen Blake receives research, conference travel, and a reduced personal commission rate from a manager whenever he refers clients there. He tells clients the relationship is “a professional courtesy” and does not describe those benefits. Which standard did Owen most likely violate?
choices: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard VI(C) Referral Fees
explanation: Non-cash benefits for referrals are still referral compensation and must be described to the client. The courtesy phrase violates Standard VI(C) Referral Fees. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because the benefits are for client referrals, not for changing a published rating. Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements is a weaker fit because the vignette’s failure is client disclosure, not the absence of a written employer consent. The strongest choice is: Standard VI(C) Referral Fees

stem: A planner will refer a prospect to Amina Shah at Westmill Fund. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Before the prospect signs, tell the prospect in plain language that Amina will pay the planner 20 percent of the first-year fee, and state that percentage and the fee.
Tell only Amina’s supervisor, and say nothing to the prospect.
Mention the arrangement a year later in a holiday card, after the prospect has already hired the firm.
explanation: Standard VI(C) Referral Fees requires disclosure of the referral compensation to the prospect, not only to the employer, in time for it to matter. Amina’s plain-language disclosure before signing complies. Employer-only notice, and a card a year later, leave the prospect in the dark when the decision is made. Those actions are worse. The strongest choice is: Before the prospect signs, tell the prospect in plain language that Amina will pay the planner 20 percent of the first-year fee, and state that percentage and the fee.

stem: After the afternoon session, Leah Bernstein posts three vignette summaries she remembers, including the company facts and the question asked, in a candidates’ group chat. Which standard did Leah most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
explanation: Specific exam content is not hers to share. Posting the vignettes violates Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs. Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program is a weaker fit because she did not misuse the designation or claim a certification. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because the wrong is exam confidentiality, not a client performance claim. The strongest choice is: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs

stem: Marcus Hale brings a formula sheet into the exam room inside a glasses case and uses it on two items. Which standard did Marcus most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(D) Misconduct
Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
Standard I(E) Competence
explanation: Using hidden notes during the exam is cheating. That violates Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs. Standard I(E) Competence is a weaker fit because a formula sheet is not how competence is maintained, and the conduct is exam misconduct. Standard I(D) Misconduct is a possible description of dishonesty, but the specific duty for exam cheating is VII(A), so it is the better fit. The strongest choice is: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs

stem: The evening of her exam, Sofia Alvarez publishes a blog post that reconstructs one item, including the answer choices. Which standard did Sofia most likely violate?
choices: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
explanation: Reconstructing a specific item, choices included, shares exam content. That violates Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs. Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is a weaker fit because the blog is not client reporting. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is a weaker fit because she did not try to move a security’s price. The strongest choice is: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs

stem: During the lunch break, Henrik Dahl studies a photo of a live item that a friend in an earlier session sent him, then returns for his own session. Which standard did Henrik most likely violate?
choices: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
Standard IV(A) Loyalty
explanation: Studying a live item before his session is cheating and misuse of exam content. That violates Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is a weaker fit because the “nonpublic” material is an exam item, not issuer information for a trade. Standard IV(A) Loyalty is a weaker fit because no employer file or client solicitation is involved. The strongest choice is: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs

stem: Jillian Crowe is asked how her exam felt, and a classmate offers a photo of an exam page. Which action is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: Say that the curriculum readings on ethics and fixed income deserved careful review, refuse the photo, and report the offer to CFA Institute.
Describe two items she found difficult, including the numbers in each vignette, because the exam day is over.
Memorize items to hand to next month’s candidates and call the notes a teaching aid.
explanation: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs forbids sharing specific exam content and cheating. A comment about curriculum areas, a refusal, and a report stay on the right side of that line. Describing vignette numbers, or passing items to later candidates, shares exam content. Those actions are worse. The strongest choice is: Say that the curriculum readings on ethics and fixed income deserved careful review, refuse the photo, and report the offer to CFA Institute.

stem: Elena Vasquez’s email signature reads “Elena Vasquez, a CFA, Senior Portfolio Manager.” Which standard did Elena most likely violate?
choices: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
explanation: The letters are not a noun. Calling herself “a CFA” violates Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program. The proper reference is “CFA charterholder,” and “Elena Vasquez, CFA” is an acceptable suffix. Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs is a weaker fit because no exam content was disclosed. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation is a weaker fit because the defective phrase is specifically about the designation. The strongest choice is: Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program

stem: Patrick Nguyen’s business card reads “Patrick Nguyen, CFA Level II.” He passed Level II and is registered for Level III. He does not hold the charter. Which standard did Patrick most likely violate?
choices: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
Standard I(E) Competence
explanation: There is no partial designation. Printing “CFA Level II” as a credential suffix violates Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program. He may say, in a sentence, that he passed Level II. Standard I(E) Competence is a weaker fit because the card is a designation problem, not a skill problem. Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs is a weaker fit because he did not cheat or reveal items. The strongest choice is: Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program

stem: A Piper Street Capital brochure says, “Returns are more reliable because our managers are CFA charterholders, so the charter stands behind the performance.” Which standard did the brochure most likely cause a member who approved it to violate?
choices: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
explanation: The charter does not guarantee or stand behind performance. Implying that it does violates Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program. Standard III(D) Performance Presentation would be stronger if the defect were a cherry-picked return. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is a weaker fit because no gift or issuer payment bent a research opinion. The strongest choice is: Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program

stem: Harbor Glass’s website banner says “Harbor Glass is certified by CFA Institute” because two employees are charterholders. Which standard did a member who approved the banner most likely violate?
choices: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
Standard I(D) Misconduct
explanation: CFA Institute does not certify firms. The banner violates Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program. Standard I(D) Misconduct is a weaker fit because the statement is a misuse of the organization’s name, which VII(B) specifically covers. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts is a weaker fit because the banner is not an ownership or board conflict. The strongest choice is: Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program

stem: Ruth Abebe holds the charter. Her colleague passed Level I of the CFA Program and is registered for Level II. Which presentation is most consistent with the Standards?
choices: The colleague’s card uses “CFA Level II candidate” as a credential suffix, and Ruth is described as “a CFA.”
The firm footer says “CFA Institute certified” the firm because two employees are charterholders.
Ruth’s card reads “Ruth Abebe, CFA,” her bio calls her a CFA charterholder, and the colleague is described only as having passed Level I of the CFA Program.
explanation: Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program allows “Ruth Abebe, CFA” and “CFA charterholder.” It does not allow “a CFA,” a partial designation suffix, or a claim that CFA Institute certified the firm. The first presentation follows those limits. The card suffix and the certification footer do not. The strongest choice is: Ruth’s card reads “Ruth Abebe, CFA,” her bio calls her a CFA charterholder, and the colleague is described only as having passed Level I of the CFA Program.

stem: A prospect is comparing two advisers who both run large-cap equity mandates. One shows a selected account. The other shows a composite built under the GIPS standards. Which purpose of the GIPS standards does the second presentation serve?
choices: It makes performance easier to compare because similar mandates are reported under a common set of rules.
It raises the expected return of the mandate by requiring a minimum alpha.
It replaces the need for an investment policy statement.
explanation: The GIPS standards exist so firms present performance in a comparable way, with rules about which accounts are included and how results are shown. They do not promise a level of alpha, and they do not take the place of a client policy statement. The strongest choice is: It makes performance easier to compare because similar mandates are reported under a common set of rules.

stem: Samuel Iqbal, a charterholder at Piper Street Capital, wants his biography to say that he complies with the GIPS standards. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: A claim of compliance is made by a firm, not by an individual.
A claim of compliance is available only to candidates who have not yet joined a firm.
Any charterholder may claim personal compliance whether or not the firm complies.
explanation: The GIPS standards are applied to a firm’s defined business, and the claim of compliance is the firm’s claim. Samuel does not become personally “GIPS compliant” by holding a charter or by managing one good account. The strongest choice is: A claim of compliance is made by a firm, not by an individual.

stem: Westmill Fund manages a small-cap value strategy and a short-duration municipal ladder. Which statement about composites is most accurate?
choices: A composite is a single representative account chosen by the marketing team each year.
A composite groups portfolios that share a similar mandate, objective, or strategy.
A composite must contain every portfolio the firm manages, regardless of strategy.
explanation: Composites are the buckets that make strategies comparable. Mixing a small-cap book with a municipal ladder would blur the strategy. A composite is not one favorite account and not an unstructured pile of every portfolio in the firm. The strongest choice is: A composite groups portfolios that share a similar mandate, objective, or strategy.

stem: Harbor Glass has twelve fee-paying discretionary portfolios that follow its written large-cap growth composite definition. Marketing wants to leave out the three that trailed the benchmark. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Only portfolios that beat the benchmark are allowed inside a composite.
All twelve must be in the composite. Fee-paying discretionary portfolios that fit the definition are not optional.
The firm may omit the three laggards if the remaining nine are still fee-paying.
explanation: Cherry-picking is the practice the composite rule is built to stop. If a portfolio is actual, fee-paying, discretionary, and fits the composite, it belongs in the composite. Trailing the benchmark is not a reason to leave it out. The strongest choice is: All twelve must be in the composite. Fee-paying discretionary portfolios that fit the definition are not optional.

stem: A pension hires Piper Street Capital as a directed broker-of-record but keeps investment discretion itself. The account pays a fee. Which treatment under the GIPS standards is most accurate?
choices: Every fee-paying account must enter a composite, including accounts the firm does not manage.
Non-discretionary accounts may be shown as the firm’s composite if they are the only accounts that made money.
A non-discretionary portfolio is not included in a composite.
explanation: Composites describe portfolios the firm actually manages. A fee-paying account is not enough when the firm lacks discretion. Putting that account into a composite, especially because the result looks good, misstates what the firm decided. The strongest choice is: A non-discretionary portfolio is not included in a composite.

stem: Two Harbor Glass accounts in a composite were closed after a weak year. A pitch book drops them so the history shows only accounts that are still open. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Terminated portfolios stay in the composite’s history for the periods the firm managed them.
Closing an account erases its history from every composite.
Terminated portfolios may be removed if the firm discloses that survivors were used.
explanation: The history of a strategy includes accounts that later left. Dropping them because they were weak, or because they are no longer on the books, rebuilds the past. Disclosure that only survivors were used does not cure the omission. The strongest choice is: Terminated portfolios stay in the composite’s history for the periods the firm managed them.

stem: Lowcountry Bank’s trust unit is preparing its first GIPS-compliant materials. The chief investment officer asks whether an outside firm must be hired before any claim of compliance. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Verification is mandatory for any firm that has more than one composite.
Verification is voluntary. A firm may claim compliance without being verified.
Verification by CFA Institute is required before the first claim of compliance.
explanation: Claiming compliance and hiring a verifier are different steps. Verification is a voluntary engagement. CFA Institute does not perform it, and the number of composites does not turn it into a requirement. The strongest choice is: Verification is voluntary. A firm may claim compliance without being verified.

stem: Iris Media’s pension consultant offers to verify Westmill Fund and also helps Westmill win the pension mandate. Which statement about the verifier is most accurate?
choices: CFA Institute is the only body allowed to verify a firm.
Verification is performed by an independent third party, not by CFA Institute and not by someone whose other role compromises that independence.
The verifier must be an employee of the firm being verified.
explanation: Independence is what makes verification useful to a prospect. The firm cannot verify itself, and CFA Institute does not act as the verifier. A party that is also selling the firm’s services into the same mandate is a poor description of an independent verifier. The strongest choice is: Verification is performed by an independent third party, not by CFA Institute and not by someone whose other role compromises that independence.

stem: A draft homepage says, “CFA Institute certified Harbor Glass under the GIPS standards.” Harbor Glass has been verified by an independent firm. Which revision is required?
choices: Keep the sentence, because a completed verification is the same thing as a CFA Institute certification.
Change only the typeface, because the problem is the font rather than the claim.
Remove the certification sentence. Verification is not a certification by CFA Institute, and firms must not say that it is.
explanation: CFA Institute does not certify firms for GIPS compliance. An independent verification is still not that certification. The homepage has to stop saying the firm was certified. Design tweaks do not fix the claim. The strongest choice is: Remove the certification sentence. Verification is not a certification by CFA Institute, and firms must not say that it is.

stem: Quill Software’s treasurer asks a Westmill Fund presenter what a verification report guarantees about the large-cap composite slide in the deck. Which answer is most accurate?
choices: Verification guarantees that every figure in every composite presentation is free of error.
Verification addresses firm-wide policies and composite construction. It is not an audit opinion on one marketing slide’s numbers.
Verification guarantees future outperformance of the composite.
explanation: Verification tests whether the firm has complied with composite-construction requirements on a firm-wide basis and whether its policies are designed to calculate and present performance in compliance. A separate performance examination would look at a specific composite. Neither engagement promises future results. The strongest choice is: Verification addresses firm-wide policies and composite construction. It is not an audit opinion on one marketing slide’s numbers.

stem: Which list belongs in a single composite at Lumen Rail’s pension manager, assuming each portfolio is fee-paying and discretionary?
choices: The liability-matching portfolios plus the firm’s venture-capital fund, so the firm has one number.
Portfolios that share the pension’s long-duration liability-matching mandate.
The one liability-matching portfolio with the highest return this year.
explanation: A composite follows a mandate, objective, or strategy. Liability-matching accounts belong together. Venture capital is a different strategy, and a single winning account is not a composite. The strongest choice is: Portfolios that share the pension’s long-duration liability-matching mandate.

stem: Piper Street Capital wants to claim GIPS compliance for its flagship fund only, while a second strategy keeps a selected-account presentation. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Flagship funds may claim compliance on their own, and other strategies are exempt.
Compliance can be claimed for any strategy that beat its benchmark in the most recent year.
A claim of compliance is firm-wide. The firm cannot claim compliance for one strategy and ignore the requirements for the rest of the defined firm.
explanation: The GIPS standards apply to the whole defined firm. Limiting the claim to a flagship, or to a strategy that recently did well, leaves the claim false even if that one strategy’s composite was built carefully. The strongest choice is: A claim of compliance is firm-wide. The firm cannot claim compliance for one strategy and ignore the requirements for the rest of the defined firm.

stem: The Code and Standards do not require a firm to follow the GIPS standards. A Harbor Glass brochure still says the firm complies, though three eligible portfolios were left out of their composite. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Following the GIPS standards is voluntary, but a firm that claims compliance must actually comply. A false claim misstates what the firm did.
Leaving portfolios out is allowed whenever the Code and Standards are also in force.
Because GIPS compliance is voluntary, a false claim of compliance is harmless.
explanation: Voluntary does not mean a firm may advertise a status it has not earned. Once Harbor Glass claims compliance, the omitted portfolios make the claim false. The Code and Standards do not create a license to cherry-pick under a GIPS banner. The strongest choice is: Following the GIPS standards is voluntary, but a firm that claims compliance must actually comply. A false claim misstates what the firm did.

stem: Who should receive a GIPS report when a firm claims compliance and a new prospect is considering a strategy?
choices: The firm must make every reasonable effort to provide a GIPS report to prospective clients, not only to consultants who already know the firm.
Only CFA charterholders on the prospect’s staff.
Only existing clients who complain about a benchmark.
explanation: The point of a claim of compliance is that prospects can see a report built under the standards. Limiting that report to angry clients, or to charterholders, defeats the comparison the standards are for. The strongest choice is: The firm must make every reasonable effort to provide a GIPS report to prospective clients, not only to consultants who already know the firm.

stem: Which statement about the name “GIPS” on a business card is most accurate?
choices: A charterholder should print “GIPS” after the CFA designation to show personal compliance.
Individuals do not append GIPS to their names the way a firm claims compliance.
Printing GIPS on a card certifies the employer.
explanation: The claim belongs to the firm and is made about the firm’s performance process. It is not a personal suffix and it does not certify the employer, just as CFA Institute does not certify firms under the standards. The strongest choice is: Individuals do not append GIPS to their names the way a firm claims compliance.

stem: A strategy launched 30 months ago. No stricter rule applies. Which presentation history is consistent with the GIPS standards’ minimum period?
choices: Wait until the strategy has ten years before showing any performance.
Show performance since inception, because the strategy does not yet have five years.
Show a ten-year record by linking a different, older strategy that was closed before this one began.
explanation: A firm presents at least five years of compliant performance, or performance since inception if the strategy is younger, and then builds the record toward ten years. Inventing length by grafting on an older, different strategy is not that history. Silence until year ten is not required. The strongest choice is: Show performance since inception, because the strategy does not yet have five years.

stem: Midway through a year, Northline Foods’ pension asks its manager to move a portfolio from the core-bond composite into the high-yield composite because high yield is having a better year. The mandate has not changed. Which response fits the GIPS standards?
choices: Move it if the pension signs a letter, even though the investment instructions are unchanged.
Move it, because composites are marketing groups and may be rearranged when a year is weak.
Keep the portfolio in the composite that matches its actual mandate. Do not move it to improve the picture.
explanation: Composite membership follows the mandate, objective, or strategy, not the year’s winners. A client letter that leaves the instructions the same does not create a new strategy. Moving the account to dress the high-yield composite is cherry-picking across time. The strongest choice is: Keep the portfolio in the composite that matches its actual mandate. Do not move it to improve the picture.

stem: Which assets are included when a GIPS-compliant firm states total firm assets?
choices: All assets managed by the defined firm, including discretionary and non-discretionary accounts and both fee-paying and non-fee-paying portfolios.
Only assets that outperformed their benchmarks.
Only the portfolios inside the flagship composite.
explanation: Total firm assets describe the defined firm, not a highlight reel. Discretion and fees affect composite membership. They do not erase assets from the firm-wide total. Outperformance is irrelevant to that total. The strongest choice is: All assets managed by the defined firm, including discretionary and non-discretionary accounts and both fee-paying and non-fee-paying portfolios.

stem: An independent verifier finishes a firm-wide verification of Piper Street Capital and does not examine the infrastructure composite. Which sentence may the firm use?
choices: The firm may say it has been verified, without saying the infrastructure composite received a performance examination or that CFA Institute certified the firm.
The firm may say every composite number was audited because verification was completed.
The firm may say CFA Institute certified the infrastructure composite because the firm was verified.
explanation: Verification and a performance examination are different. Verification can be described as verification.
